# Article 1(2)(a)–(b) threshold excess calculation (Reg. (EC) No 139/2004)

## 1. Scope and legal basis

Computation only: for each recorded turnover figure supplied by the filing team, the arithmetic difference between that figure and the corresponding turnover threshold in Article 1(2) of Council Regulation (EC) No 139/2004 (the EC Merger Regulation), OJ L 24, 29.1.2004, p. 1.

Operative text relied on (Art. 1(2)):

> "2. A concentration has a Community dimension where:
> (a) the combined aggregate worldwide turnover of all the undertakings concerned is more than EUR 5 000 million; and
> (b) the aggregate Community-wide turnover of each of at least two of the undertakings concerned is more than EUR 250 million,
> unless each of the undertakings concerned achieves more than two-thirds of its aggregate Community-wide turnover within one and the same Member State."

## 2. Thresholds applied and why

| Limb | Threshold applied | Source / status |
|---|---|---|
| Art. 1(2)(a) — combined aggregate worldwide turnover, all undertakings concerned | EUR 5,000 million | Reg. 139/2004 Art. 1(2)(a), in force |
| Art. 1(2)(b) — aggregate Community-wide turnover, each of at least two undertakings concerned | EUR 250 million (same figure applied to each undertaking) | Reg. 139/2004 Art. 1(2)(b), in force |

Notes on threshold selection:

- The ECU 5,000 million / ECU 250 million figures appearing in the Commission's threshold-review material are the figures of the predecessor Regulation (EEC) No 4064/89 and are not the figures applicable to a check under Reg. 139/2004. The 2004 Regulation expresses the thresholds in EUR.
- Article 1(4) of Reg. 139/2004 provides for possible adjustment of the thresholds; no such adjustment has been adopted, so the EUR 5,000 million / EUR 250 million figures remain the thresholds in force. If a future Art. 1(4) adjustment takes effect before the relevant date, each excess below must be recomputed against the adjusted figures (excess = recorded amount − adjusted threshold).
- The Article 1(3) alternative thresholds (EUR 2,500 million / EUR 100 million / EUR 25 million / EUR 100 million) are not part of this check and are not applied.
- Currency: all recorded amounts and all thresholds are stated in EUR millions; no conversion is performed. If any recorded figure were in another currency, it would first have to be converted to EUR (Art. 5(1) uses the average of the exchange rates prevailing in the financial year concerned) before subtraction.
- The amounts are taken at face value as recorded. No Article 5 adjustment (deduction of intra-group turnover, re-attribution of turnover of joint ventures or of undertakings in which rights or powers listed in Art. 5(4)(b) are held, geographic allocation) is performed.

## 3. Computation

Excess = recorded amount − corresponding threshold (both in EUR millions). Because Art. 1(2) uses "more than", a positive difference means the recorded amount is above the threshold; the excess is stated as an absolute amount, not a ratio.

| # | Recorded amount (EUR m) | Corresponding threshold (EUR m) | Excess (EUR m) | Limb |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 5,400 (combined aggregate worldwide turnover, all undertakings concerned) | 5,000 | **400** | Art. 1(2)(a) |
| 2 | 300 (aggregate Community-wide turnover, undertaking 1) | 250 | **50** | Art. 1(2)(b) |
| 3 | 275 (aggregate Community-wide turnover, undertaking 2) | 250 | **25** | Art. 1(2)(b) |

Arithmetic shown explicitly:

- Worldwide limb: 5,400 − 5,000 = **400 EUR million** above the Art. 1(2)(a) threshold.
- Community-wide limb, undertaking 1: 300 − 250 = **50 EUR million** above the Art. 1(2)(b) threshold.
- Community-wide limb, undertaking 2: 275 − 250 = **25 EUR million** above the Art. 1(2)(b) threshold.

All three differences are positive; none is negative or zero, so in each case the recorded amount is strictly above the threshold as recorded (subject to the reservation in section 4).

## 4. Express reservation — no conclusion on Community dimension

This memorandum does **not** determine whether the concentration has a Community dimension, and nothing in it should be read as such a determination. In particular:

- The two-thirds rule in the closing words of Art. 1(2)(b)(ii) is not assessed. A concentration meeting the two turnover figures in Art. 1(2)(a) and (b) does not have a Community dimension if each undertaking concerned achieves more than two-thirds of its aggregate Community-wide turnover within one and the same Member State. The arithmetic in section 3 says nothing about that condition.
- The Art. 1(3) alternative thresholds are not assessed.
- Whether the recorded figures are the correct turnover figures for Art. 1(2) purposes (Art. 5 computation, geographic allocation, undertakings concerned) is not assessed; the figures are taken as recorded.
- The computation states only the arithmetic excess of each recorded amount over the corresponding threshold. It is a threshold-arithmetic input for the filing team, not a jurisdictional conclusion.

## 5. Reporting convention

Excesses are reported as absolute amounts in EUR millions (recorded amount minus threshold), separately for each limb and each undertaking, so that the reader can see which limb each figure relates to. Percentage or ratio expressions are not used.

question: Y134

LEGAL OPINION — Aggregation of two simultaneously concluded off-premises contracts for the EUR 50 optional exclusion (Art. 3(4), Directive 2011/83/EU)

I. QUESTIONS ANSWERED
(1) What total is used for the threshold? — EUR 55 (EUR 30 + EUR 25).
(2) Does the optional exclusion cover this pair on that basis? — No. EUR 55 exceeds the EUR 50 ceiling, so the exclusion is unavailable and both contracts remain within the Directive.

II. LEGAL BASIS (text relied on)
Art. 3(4) Dir. 2011/83/EU: 'Member States may decide not to apply this Directive or not to maintain or introduce corresponding national provisions to off-premises contracts for which the payment to be made by the consumer does not exceed EUR 50. Member States may define a lower value in their national legislation.'

Recital 28 Dir. 2011/83/EU: 'In order to avoid administrative burden being placed on traders, Member States may decide not to apply this Directive where goods or services of a minor value are sold off-premises. The monetary threshold should be established at a sufficiently low level as to exclude only purchases of small significance. Member States should be allowed to define this value in their national legislation provided that it does not exceed EUR 50. Where two or more contracts with related subjects are concluded at the same time by the consumer, the total cost thereof should be taken into account for the purpose of applying this threshold.'

Art. 4 (level of harmonisation) confirms that where the Directive applies, a Member State cannot water down or vary the protective provisions; the only latitude here is the Art. 3(4) option itself, exercisable downwards only (a lower value, never above EUR 50).

III. STEP-BY-STEP APPLICATION
Step 1 — Is the exclusion available in this Member State? Yes, on the stated facts the Member State has opted in at the maximum permitted value of EUR 50. The ceiling is therefore EUR 50.

Step 2 — Is the threshold assessed per contract or across the transaction? Across the transaction, where the conditions of Recital 28 are met. Recital 28 is the only Union-level rule addressing multi-contract situations, and it is directly on point: it supplies the method for 'applying this threshold' when 'two or more contracts with related subjects are concluded at the same time by the consumer'. Art. 3(4)'s 'payment to be made by the consumer' is read in the light of that method; recitals are the standard interpretative aid for the operative provisions and there is no contrary operative text.

Step 3 — Do the Recital 28 conditions hold here?
 (a) 'two or more contracts' — yes, two.
 (b) 'with related subjects' — yes on the stated premise that the two contracts are related in subject matter (the relatedness is to the subject matter, not to the identity of the trader; two contracts with the same trader on unrelated subjects would not aggregate, and related subjects with associated traders would).
 (c) 'concluded at the same time' — yes, simultaneous conclusion is stated.
All three conditions are satisfied, so aggregation is mandatory for the threshold calculation.

Step 4 — Compute the total. EUR 30 + EUR 25 = EUR 55. The threshold figure is EUR 55. Neither EUR 30 nor EUR 25 is tested separately.

Step 5 — Apply the test. Art. 3(4) requires that the payment 'does not exceed EUR 50'. EUR 55 > EUR 50. The condition is not met.

IV. CONCLUSION
- Threshold total: EUR 55.
- Verdict: the optional off-premises exclusion does NOT cover this pair. Identifier: NO_NOT_COVERED.
- Consequence: both contracts remain inside the Directive. The trader owes the Chapter III off-premises regime for each: the Art. 6 information requirements, the Art. 7 formal requirements (including the model withdrawal form and the confirmation under Art. 7(2)), and the consumer has the Art. 9 right of withdrawal (14 days from delivery/conclusion as applicable). The exclusion, had it applied, would have disapplied the Directive in its entirety — information duties and withdrawal right alike; it is all-or-nothing and cannot be applied to one contract of the pair and not the other, because the threshold is measured on the aggregated total.

V. WHY THE CONTRARY VIEW FAILS
An argument that each contract is tested alone (EUR 30 and EUR 25, each under EUR 50) would make Recital 28 inoperative: the recital exists precisely to stop the threshold being defeated by splitting a single small-value transaction into several contracts with related subjects concluded at the same time. It would also invert the recital's stated rationale — the exclusion is meant to spare traders the burden of 'purchases of small significance', and a EUR 55 basket is not made insignificant by being papered into two documents. Per-contract assessment would additionally reward the very structuring the recital forbids, which is why aggregation is treated as part of the method of applying the threshold rather than as a discretionary gloss.

VI. CALIBRATION NOTES (consistency of the figures stated above)
- Ceiling applied: EUR 50 (maximum permitted; Member States may only go lower).
- Test: 'does not exceed EUR 50' — i.e. EUR 50 exactly is still inside the exclusion; EUR 50.01 is not.
- Illustrative counter-case: contracts of EUR 30 and EUR 20 aggregate to EUR 50, which does not exceed EUR 50, so the exclusion would apply to both. This confirms the boundary is inclusive and that the EUR 55 outcome above turns on exceeding, not on reaching, the ceiling.
- Currency/VAT: the figures are taken as the 'payment to be made by the consumer' under each contract. If a national measure or the contract documents show the threshold is computed on a different base (e.g. a VAT-exclusive price, or a price net of delivery or ancillary charges), the aggregate must be recomputed on that base; a EUR 55 total would need to fall to EUR 50 or below to change the verdict, which requires a reduction of more than EUR 5 across the pair.

VII. PREMISES AND VERIFICATION POINTS (flagging, not assuming away)
This opinion rests on: (i) both contracts being off-premises contracts within Art. 2(8); (ii) the EUR 30 and EUR 25 being the full prices used for threshold purposes; (iii) the national implementing measure mirroring the EUR 50 ceiling without a lower value; (iv) the two subject matters being 'related' and the contracts being concluded at the same time. Points (iii) and (iv) are the ones to verify against the actual national transposition text and the contract documents before relying on this opinion in a live matter; if the national measure has set a lower value, the exclusion is even less available and the verdict is unchanged; if the subject matters are in fact unrelated, the aggregation falls away and each contract would be tested at EUR 30 and EUR 25 respectively, in which case both would fall inside the exclusion and the Directive would not apply to either. National case law and administrative guidance on simultaneity and relatedness should be checked in the specific Member State, as the Directive does not define either term.

answer:
# MEMORANDUM — Status of the Appendix of Forms to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, and Correction of a 2014 Manual's Reference

**Scope note (Legal Researcher):** This is a research memorandum. It states the governing law as of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure amended to December 1, 2025, and supplies ready-to-apply redline language for the manual. It is not a filing and needs review by supervising counsel before publication.

---

## I. BOTTOM LINE

1. **Status as of the rules amended to December 1, 2025: the Appendix of Forms has been ABROGATED.** It is not relocated, not merely renumbered, and not superseded in place. The current FRCP contain no Appendix of Forms, and the forms formerly printed there carry no rule-based authority.
2. **Effective date of that change: December 1, 2015** — adopted by Supreme Court order dated April 29, 2015, transmitted to Congress under 28 U.S.C. § 2074, no congressional action, effective December 1, 2015. The same order abrogated **Rule 84**, the rule that had given the appendix its operative effect.
3. **The December 1, 2025 amendments did NOT touch the appendix.** Those amendments are Rules 16 and 26 and new Rule 16.1 only. So the correct statement is: *as of December 1, 2025, the appendix has been gone for ten years.* A 2014 manual is therefore wrong twice over — it is pre-abrogation and pre-dates the 2015 package, the 2016–2025 amendments, and the 2025 restyling of Rules 16/26.

---

## II. ASK 2 — STATUS OF THE APPENDIX OF FORMS

### A. Holding

As amended to December 1, 2025, the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure contain **no Appendix of Forms**. The appendix was **abrogated**, effective December 1, 2015, together with **Rule 84**.

### B. Textual proof from the current official text

The official Judicial Conference text of the FRCP, amended to December 1, 2025, prints:

> "Rule 84. [Abrogated (Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).]"

Two points follow directly from that line:

- The abrogation is **bracketed and dated in the current text**, i.e., it is part of the operative rule set the manual's users are governed by today — not a pending or proposed change.
- The parenthetical supplies both the **adopting order date (April 29, 2015)** and the **effective date (December 1, 2015)**.

Rule 84 was the provision that gave the appendix its bite (in its last form, it provided that the forms in the appendix "suffice under these rules" and illustrate the simplicity and brevity the rules contemplate). Abrogating the appendix while abrogating Rule 84 is what removed the forms' rule-based safe harbor; it is not a cosmetic renumbering.

### C. Corroboration from the rulemaking record

The Federal Judicial Center's amendment history, under the heading **"Effective December 1, 2015,"** records the amendments package transmitted to Congress as covering:

> "the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (rules 1, 4, 16, 26, 30, 31, 33, 34, 37, and 55 **and the abrogation of rule 84 and the appendix of forms**)."

That entry confirms three things at once: (i) the appendix was **abrogated** (the record's own word), (ii) it was part of a **package**, not a standalone repeal, and (iii) the package is dated **December 1, 2015**.

### D. What abrogation does and does not mean — the distinction the manual needs

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Was the appendix **moved** elsewhere in the FRCP? | No. There is no successor "Appendix" in the Civil Rules. |
| Was it **superseded** by a new forms set in the rules? | No. The Civil Rules contain no Official Forms set comparable to the Bankruptcy Official Forms. |
| Do the **functions** the old forms served still exist? | Yes — but as **Administrative Office / Director's forms and national court forms**, not as rule appendices. |
| Does tracking an old form still **guarantee** a pleading suffices? | No. Former Rule 84's safe harbor is gone; sufficiency is governed by Rule 8(a)(2) and Rule 12(b)(6) as construed in *Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly* and *Ashcroft v. Iqbal*. |
| Are the **Bankruptcy Official Forms** affected? | No — different set, separately prescribed and still mandatory in bankruptcy cases. Do not let the manual conflate the two. |

**Surviving forms, mapped by function** (map by function, not by former number — old numbering shifted across editions and should not be reproduced without checking the manual's own edition):

| Function formerly served by an appendix form | Current source |
|---|---|
| Summons in a civil action | AO Form 440 |
| Notice of a lawsuit and request to waive service of a summons | AO Form 398 |
| Waiver of the service of a summons | AO Form 399 |
| Notice, consent, and reference of a civil action to a magistrate judge | AO Form 85 |
| Model complaint / model answer (the old illustrative pleading forms) | **No replacement form.** Use Rule 8(a) and Rule 12; the manual's own exemplars are illustrative only. |

These AO/Director's forms are administrative instruments posted on the judiciary's forms pages. Using or not using them has no rule-based legal consequence of the kind former Rule 84 supplied.

---

## III. ASK 3 — WHEN THE CHANGE TOOK EFFECT

### A. Holding

**December 1, 2015.**

### B. Rulemaking path (Rules Enabling Act, 28 U.S.C. §§ 2071–2074)

1. **Advisory Committee / Standing Committee** proposed the 2015 Civil Rules package, which included abrogation of Rule 84 and the Appendix of Forms.
2. **Supreme Court order dated April 29, 2015** adopted the amendments and the abrogations.
3. **Transmitted to Congress** under 28 U.S.C. § 2074.
4. **Congress took no action** within the statutory review period.
5. **Effective December 1, 2015**, per the terms of the order and § 2074.

### C. Application to cases already pending on December 1, 2015

Rule 86(a) governs: the amendments took effect on the date specified by the Supreme Court and govern proceedings commenced after that date and, in actions then pending, proceedings after that date unless the Court specifies otherwise or the court determines application would be infeasible or work an injustice. Practically: the abrogation of the forms does not invalidate anything filed while the forms existed, but no party can now invoke the former Rule 84 safe harbor.

### D. What did NOT happen on December 1, 2025

The December 1, 2025 amendments are limited to **Civil Rules 16 and 26 and new Rule 16.1** (Supreme Court order dated April 23, 2025; effective December 1, 2025; governing all proceedings thereafter commenced and, insofar as just and practicable, all proceedings then pending). The judiciary's own list of everything effective December 1, 2025 (Appellate Rules 6 and 39; Bankruptcy Rules 3002.1 and 8006; the listed bankruptcy forms; Civil Rules 16 and 26 and new Rule 16.1) contains **no appendix item**. Do not let the manual's reviser write "the appendix was abolished effective December 1, 2025" — that is the single most likely error in this correction.

---

## IV. CORRECTING THE 2014 MANUAL

### A. Edit protocol

1. **Search strings** across the full text, tables of authorities, index, and forms lists: `Appendix of Forms`; `Appendix`; `Rule 84`; `Form 1`; `Form 1A`; `Form 1B`; `Form 2`; `Form 3`; `Form 4`; `Form 5`; `Form 6`; `Form 11`; `Form 18`; `Form 19`; `Form 34`; `Form 52`; `Form 70`; `Form 71`; `Form 72`; `Official Form`; `official form`; `suffice`; `simplicity and brevity`.
2. **Classify each hit** as (a) a citation to a former appendix form, (b) a substantive statement that the forms have rule-based effect, or (c) a reference to a still-existing AO/Director's form. Handle (a) and (b) with the replacements below; leave (c) alone but verify the form number is current.
3. **Replace by function** using the table in § II.D. Never substitute one former form number for another.
4. **Delete every statement that a pleading "suffices" because it tracks an official form.** Substitute the Rule 8(a)(2)/*Twombly*/*Iqbal* formulation.
5. **Insert the standing footnote** (below) at the first surviving mention of the old forms and in the manual's table of authorities.
6. **Audit derivative material**: local rules, standing orders, chambers checklists, and appendix/tab sets that the manual reproduces or cross-references may themselves quote former form numbers. Flag them for separate review; do not silently "correct" a court's own local rule text.
7. **Add a currency statement** on the copyright/edition page: "Rules text current through amendments effective December 1, 2025."

### B. Model footnote (drop in verbatim)

> The Appendix of Forms to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and Rule 84 were abrogated by order of the Supreme Court dated April 29, 2015, effective December 1, 2015. The forms formerly printed in the appendix no longer have the force of rule text, and no pleading is sufficient merely because it tracks a former form. Pleading sufficiency is governed by Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a)(2) and 12(b)(6). The summons and waiver-of-service forms in current use are Administrative Office forms (AO 440, AO 398, AO 399), not rule appendices.

### C. Model redline for a typical sentence

- **2014 text:** "A complaint in substantially the form set out in Form 11 of the Appendix of Forms suffices under Rule 84."
- **Corrected text:** "No official complaint form is prescribed. A complaint must contain 'a short and plain statement of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled to relief,' Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a)(2), and must satisfy the plausibility standard of *Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly*, 550 U.S. 544 (2007), and *Ashcroft v. Iqbal*, 556 U.S. 662 (2009). The model complaint in this chapter is illustrative only and carries no rule-based authority."

- **2014 text:** "Serve the waiver request in the form of Form 1A."
- **Corrected text:** "The notice and request for waiver of service must satisfy Fed. R. Civ. P. 4(d). The Administrative Office's AO Form 398 (Notice of a Lawsuit and Request to Waive Service of a Summons) and AO Form 399 (Waiver of the Service of a Summons) are available for this purpose but are not prescribed by the Civil Rules."

### D. Currency warning to include in the revision memo

A 2014 edition pre-dates not only the 2015 abrogation but the entire 2015 Civil Rules package (Rules 1, 4, 16, 26, 30, 31, 33, 34, 37, 55), every amendment cycle from 2016 through 2024, and the December 1, 2025 amendments to Rules 16 and 26 and new Rule 16.1. Correcting the appendix reference alone will leave the manual materially stale. Recommend a full currency review of the rules-based chapters, prioritized by: Rule 26 discovery (amended 2015 and again 2025), Rule 16 scheduling (2015 and 2025), Rule 1 (2015), and the 2025 addition of Rule 16.1 on multidistrict litigation.

---

## V. RESIDUAL VERIFICATION ITEMS (do not affect the answers above)

1. **Foreword boilerplate.** The current volume's foreword still recites that the document contains the rules "together with forms." That is legacy boilerplate carried forward from pre-2015 editions. It does not reinstate the Appendix of Forms; the operative text (Rule 84 bracketed as abrogated) controls. If the reviser wants to describe what forms, if any, are physically printed in the current pamphlet (e.g., maritime Supplemental Rules forms), confirm against the pamphlet's table of contents before writing about it — and do not describe any such forms as "the Appendix of Forms."
2. **Committee Note language.** The Advisory Committee's note accompanying the 2015 abrogation explains the rationale (including that the forms had come to be over-read as definitive statements of pleading sufficiency, and that abrogation does not alter pleading standards). Pull the exact sentences from the Committee Note — reprinted in the Appendix to Title 28, United States Code, following Rule 84 — before quoting it in the manual. Paraphrase is used above; do not attribute quoted language to the note until verified.
3. **Former form numbers.** The manual's own edition governs which numbers it used. Identify each citation by function and map with § II.D rather than assuming a numbering scheme.
4. **Local materials.** Check whether any local rule or standing order the manual reproduces incorporates a former form by number; that is a court's text to amend, not the manual's.

---

## VI. TABLE OF AUTHORITIES

**Statutes**
- 28 U.S.C. § 2072 (Rules Enabling Act — power to prescribe).
- 28 U.S.C. § 2074 (congressional review; December 1 effective date absent congressional action).

**Supreme Court orders**
- Order dated April 29, 2015 (2015 Civil Rules package; abrogation of Rule 84 and the Appendix of Forms; effective December 1, 2015).
- Order dated April 23, 2025 (Rules 16 and 26 amended; new Rule 16.1; effective December 1, 2025).

**Rules**
- Fed. R. Civ. P. 84 — "[Abrogated (Apr. 29, 2015, eff. Dec. 1, 2015).]"
- Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a)(2); Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(6); Fed. R. Civ. P. 4(d); Fed. R. Civ. P. 86(a).

**Cases**
- *Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly*, 550 U.S. 544 (2007).
- *Ashcroft v. Iqbal*, 556 U.S. 662 (2009).

**Secondary / official sources**
- Judicial Conference of the United States, *Federal Rules of Civil Procedure* (amended to Dec. 1, 2025), Foreword and Rule 84 text.
- Federal Judicial Center, *Recent Amendments to the Federal Rules of Practice and Procedure*, entry under "Effective December 1, 2015" ("the abrogation of rule 84 and the appendix of forms").
- uscourts.gov, *Current Rules of Practice & Procedure* (listing rules and forms effective December 1, 2025: Appellate Rules 6 and 39; Bankruptcy Rules 3002.1 and 8006; Bankruptcy Official Forms 410S1, 410C13-M1, 410C13-M1R, 410C13-N, 410C13-NR, 410C13-M2, 410C13-M2R; Civil Rules 16 and 26 and new Rule 16.1).

# Legal opinion — term of office of judges of the European Court of Human Rights under the Convention as amended through Protocol No. 15

## 1. Scope and source (satisfies ask 1)

This opinion is confined to the Convention text **presented as amended through Protocol No. 15**. The version used is the Council of Europe / Court consolidated text issued under the Protocol No. 15 watermark:

- *Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, as amended by Protocols No. 11, 14 and 15* — consolidated watermarked text, «Convention_Watermark_P15_ENG», European Court of Human Rights, https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Convention_Watermark_P15_ENG. The text carries the endorsement **“Entry into force: 01/08/2021”** (printed at the foot of the Article 26 page), i.e. the date of entry into force of Protocol No. 15 (CETS 213).

Two further Council of Europe documents are used only to **corroborate** the same wording, not to substitute for it:
- PACE, Committee on Legal Affairs and Human Rights, *Procedure for electing judges*, AS/Jur/Inf (2014) 03 rev, https://www.assembly.coe.int/CommitteeDocs/2014/ajinfdoc03_2014.pdf
- Secretary General of the Parliamentary Assembly, SG-AS (2026) 01, *Procedure for the election of judges to the European Court of Human Rights*, https://rm.coe.int/procedure-for-the-election-of-judges-to-the-european-court-of-human-ri/1680aa8ddf

Reference is also made to Protocol No. 14 (CETS 194) as reproduced in the Council of Europe library collection, https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/library_collection_p14_ets194e_eng — solely to date the change correctly (see §5).

## 2. The operative provision, quoted verbatim

Article 23 of the consolidated P15 text reads in full:

> **ARTICLE 23 — Terms of office and dismissal**
> 1. The judges shall be elected for a period of **nine years**. They **may not be re-elected**.
> 2. The judges shall hold office until replaced. They shall, however, continue to deal with such cases as they already have under consideration.
> 3. No judge may be dismissed from office unless the other judges decide by a majority of two-thirds that that judge has ceased to fulfil the required conditions.

The two operative words for this query are in the first sentence of paragraph 1, and they are unambiguous: a **single, non-renewable term**.

## 3. Answer to ask 2 — what is the election term

**Nine years.**

“The judges shall be elected for a period of nine years.” (Article 23 §1, P15 consolidated text.)

This is a fixed term attached to the election; it is not a maximum, not a probationary period, and not subject to renewal. Article 23 §2 adds only that a judge whose seat is not yet filled *holds office until replaced*, and continues to deal with cases already under consideration — a continuity rule, not an extension of the term.

## 4. Answer to ask 3 — may a judge be re-elected

**No.**

“They may not be re-elected.” (Article 23 §1, second sentence, P15 consolidated text.)

A judge of the Court serves one term of nine years and cannot be elected to the Court for a second term. The prohibition is on **re-election as a judge of the Court**; it says nothing about eligibility for any other office (e.g. President of a Chamber under Article 25, which is expressly renewable — “they may be re-elected” — or any national or international post). That distinction should be kept in the slide correction so the rule is not over-read.

## 5. Corroboration and one historical precision that matters for the correction

**Corroboration (three independent Council of Europe sources, identical wording):**

| Source | Wording |
|---|---|
| Consolidated P15 text, Art. 23 §1 | “The judges shall be elected for a period of nine years. They may not be re-elected.” |
| AS/Jur/Inf (2014) 03 rev, §4 | “1. The judges shall be elected for a period of nine years. They may not be re-elected.” |
| SG-AS (2026) 01, §13 (“Article 23 of the Convention, as amended by Protocol No. 15”) | “1. The judges shall be elected for a period of nine years. They may not be re-elected.” |

**The historical precision.** The slide's “six-year renewable” rule is not merely pre-Protocol-15; it is pre-Protocol-14. Protocol No. 14 (CETS 194, in force **1 June 2010**) already replaced Article 23 with:

> “Article 23 – Terms of office and dismissal
> 1 The judges shall be elected for a period of nine years. They may not be re-elected.
> 2 The terms of office of judges shall expire when they reach the age of 70. […]”

and its Article 21 provided transitional extensions (first-term judges extended ipso jure to nine years; other judges' terms extended by two years). The PACE information document states this expressly: “Amending Protocol No. 14 to the Convention, in force since 1 June 2010, instituted a single term of office of nine years for judges elected to the Court…”

**What Protocol No. 15 then did to Article 23** was *not* to create the nine-year rule but to (i) **delete the age-70 expiry** formerly in Article 23 §2 and (ii) shift the age condition upstream into Article 21 §2 (candidates must be less than 65 at the date the list of three is requested). The consolidated P15 text shows exactly this: Article 23 now has three paragraphs, no age limit; Article 21 §2 carries the 65-year candidacy rule; and the SG-AS note records “Former paragraph 2 of Article 23 (‘The terms of office of judges shall expire when they reach the age of 70’) was deleted by Protocol 15.” The Protocol No. 15 explanatory report confirms the rationale and, in passing, the non-renewability: “It was considered no longer essential to impose an age limit, given the fact that judges' terms of office are no longer renewable.”

Practical consequence for the slide: the “six-year renewable” statement has been wrong since **1 June 2010**, and remains wrong under the P15 text now in force (since **1 August 2021**). The correction should not say “Protocol No. 15 introduced nine-year terms” — that would be a second, different error. It should say the nine-year single term comes from Protocol No. 14, and Protocol No. 15 removed the age-70 expiry and added the age-65 candidacy condition.

**Transitional note and its limit.** The text itself attaches the nine-year, non-renewable rule to *election*, so judges elected before 1 August 2021 on six-year renewable terms served out the terms on which they were elected (as extended under Protocol No. 14 Article 21), and the new rule governs elections taking place after entry into force. I flag honestly that the passages retrieved for this opinion do **not** include the explanatory report's commentary corresponding to Article 3 of the amending Protocol (the Article 23 amendment), so I do not assert any further transitional rule. This limit does not touch either answer: the term and the non-renewability are stated verbatim in the governing text.

## 6. Corroborating provisions (for the slide's footnote)

- **Article 22** (unchanged in the relevant part by Protocol No. 15, which deleted only its paragraph 2): judges are elected by the Parliamentary Assembly by a majority of votes cast, from a list of three candidates nominated by the High Contracting Party.
- **Article 21 §2** (inserted by Protocol No. 15): candidates must be less than 65 years of age at the date the list of three is requested.
- **Article 21 §4**: judges may not, during their term of office, engage in any activity incompatible with independence, impartiality or the demands of a full-time office.
- **Article 23 §3**: removal only by a two-thirds majority of the other judges.
- **Article 25**: by contrast, the President, Vice-Presidents and Chamber Presidents are elected for three years and “may be re-elected” — a useful contrast to show trainees that non-renewability is specific to the judicial term.

## 7. Deliverable — replacement slide text and note to the slide owner

**Current slide (to be withdrawn):** “Judges of the European Court of Human Rights serve renewable six-year terms.”

**Replacement slide text:**

> **Term of office of ECHR judges (Article 23, Convention as amended through Protocol No. 15)**
> - Elected for a **single term of nine years**.
> - **Not re-eligible**: “They may not be re-elected.”
> - They hold office until replaced and continue to deal with cases already under consideration.
> - Removal only by a two-thirds majority of the other judges.
> - *Source: Article 23 §1–3, Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms as amended by Protocols No. 11, 14 and 15 (consolidated P15 text, entry into force 1 August 2021).*

**Note to the slide owner (short form):**

> The “renewable six-year term” was correct only until 31 May 2010. Protocol No. 14 (in force 1 June 2010) replaced it with a single nine-year term, non-renewable. Protocol No. 15 (in force 1 August 2021) kept the nine-year non-renewable term, deleted the age-70 expiry from Article 23 §2 and moved the age condition into Article 21 §2 (candidates under 65 at the date the list of three is requested). Please replace the slide; the governing words are “elected for a period of nine years. They may not be re-elected.”

**Suggested footnote citation:** Article 23 §§1–3, Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, as amended by Protocols No. 11, 14 and 15 (consolidated text, Council of Europe/ECHR, entry into force 1 August 2021); cf. Article 21 §2 and Article 22.

## 8. One-line answers

- **Election term:** nine years (Article 23 §1, first sentence).
- **Re-election:** not permitted (Article 23 §1, second sentence).
- **The slide:** outdated — wrong since 1 June 2010 (Protocol No. 14), not merely since 1 August 2021 (Protocol No. 15).

LEGAL NOTE — Applicability of Commission Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 (GBER) to aid facilitating the closure of uncompetitive coal mines

1. QUESTIONS PRESENTED
(1) May a State-aid team rely on Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 to exempt aid to facilitate the closure of an uncompetitive coal mine from the notification obligation in Article 108(3) TFEU?
(2) If not, which instrument does the Regulation's scope passage identify as dealing with that aid?

2. SHORT ANSWERS
(1) NO. Aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines is expressly carved out of the GBER's scope. It is not block-exempted and must be notified.
(2) Council Decision No 2010/787/EU of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines (cited in the Regulation as 'Council Decision No 2010/787').

3. THE OPERATIVE TEXT
3.1 Article 1(3)(d) GBER (scope — excluded sectors), as adopted on 17 June 2014 and reproduced in the consolidated text:

  '3. This Regulation shall not apply to:
   ...
   (d) aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines, as covered by Council Decision No 2010/787;
   ...'

3.2 Recital 12 GBER (same rule, stated as rationale):

  '(12) This Regulation should not apply to aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines, which is dealt with by the Council Decision of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines. This Regulation should apply to other types of aid in the coal sector, with the exception of regional aid.'

3.3 Article 2(13) GBER cross-refers to the same instrument for the definition of 'coal':

  "(13) 'coal' means high-grade, medium-grade and low-grade category A and B coal within the meaning of the international codification system for coal established by the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe and clarified in the Council decision of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines ..."

4. ANALYSIS
4.1 The GBER is a block-exemption instrument: it declares certain categories of aid compatible with the internal market and thereby dispenses with the notification requirement of Article 108(3) TFEU. Its benefit is available only for aid that falls within its scope. Article 1 fixes that scope, and Article 1(3) lists sectors and purposes to which the Regulation 'shall not apply'.

4.2 Coal-mine closure aid is one of those excluded categories. The exclusion is drafted as a categorical disapplication ('shall not apply to'), not as a conditional or threshold-based limitation. There is accordingly no aid intensity, notification threshold, or set of conditions within the GBER under which closure aid for an uncompetitive coal mine could be brought back inside the block exemption. A State-aid team therefore cannot issue a GBER-based exemption decision for such aid, cannot rely on the GBER's notification-free route, and cannot cure the position by structuring the measure to satisfy GBER conditions (for example by re-labelling it as regional, environmental or training aid) where the substance is closure aid to a coal mine.

4.3 Recital 12 confirms the design and supplies the pointer: the matter 'is dealt with by' the Council Decision of 10 December 2010. Article 1(3)(d) names the same instrument in the operative provision, using its Council document number: Council Decision No 2010/787. Article 2(13) reinforces the link by defining 'coal' by reference to that Decision.

4.4 The correct legal route is therefore: assess the measure against Council Decision 2010/787/EU (the lex specialis adopted under Article 107(3)(e) TFEU for coal), and notify it to the Commission under Article 108(3) TFEU. The Decision, not the GBER, supplies the compatibility criteria (categories of aid: operating aid to loss-making mines under a closure plan, aid covering exceptional costs, inherited liabilities; and the closure deadline and degressivity rules).

4.5 Two qualifications matter for the team's file:
(a) Severability. The final subparagraph of Article 1(3) provides that where an undertaking is active both in an excluded sector and in sectors within the GBER's scope, the Regulation applies to aid for the latter activities, provided the Member State ensures by appropriate means (separation of activities, distinction of costs) that the excluded activities do not benefit. A diversified beneficiary can therefore still receive GBER-covered aid for its non-coal activities — but not for the mine closure itself.
(b) Other coal-sector aid. Recital 12, second sentence, makes clear the Regulation does apply to 'other types of aid in the coal sector, with the exception of regional aid'. Aid to a coal undertaking that is not closure aid (for example certain R&D, environmental, training or SME measures) may therefore be GBER-eligible on the ordinary conditions, subject to that regional-aid carve-out. The dividing line is whether the aid's purpose is to facilitate closure of an uncompetitive mine; if it is, Article 1(3)(d) applies regardless of its formal label.

5. CONSEQUENCES OF PROCEEDING ON A GBER BASIS (what to tell the granting authority)
5.1 Because the aid is outside the block exemption, it is notifiable and the standstill obligation in the last sentence of Article 108(3) TFEU applies in full. Aid granted without notification and authorisation is unlawful.
5.2 An unlawful aid finding exposes the measure to recovery from the beneficiary, with interest, under Article 16 of Council Regulation (EU) 2015/1589, and the national granting decision is vulnerable before national courts. A block-exemption 'declaration' in a granting decision does not cure this; it is a misapplication of Article 1(3)(d).
5.3 Internal quality control: the team's exemption checklist should carry a hard stop for Article 1(3) sectors, with coal-mine closure routed to a notification file rather than an exemption file.

6. VERSION / TEMPORAL CAVEATS (verify before relying in a live file)
6.1 The Article 1(3)(d) carve-out and recital 12 are present in the original text as adopted (17 June 2014) and have been carried unchanged through the successive amendments of the GBER. The identification of the other instrument as Council Decision 2010/787 is therefore stable across versions. The team should nevertheless cite the consolidated version in force on the date of the granting decision.
6.2 Council Decision 2010/787/EU was itself time-limited: it applied until 31 December 2020 (its Article 13). This note answers the question asked — which instrument the GBER's scope passage identifies — and that answer is Council Decision 2010/787. But if the aid in question is to be granted after the Decision's expiry, the Decision cannot supply the legal basis either, and the measure would have to be assessed directly against Article 107(3) TFEU (in practice, on the Commission's coal-closure assessment practice) and notified. Confirm the Decision's expiry provision and any transitional arrangements against the text before advising on a post-2020 grant.
6.3 Whether the mine is 'uncompetitive' and the aid is genuinely 'to facilitate closure' are questions of fact and characterisation under the Council Decision's own criteria; they do not affect the GBER answer, because the exclusion bites on the category, not on whether the conditions would be met.

7. CITATIONS
- Commission Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 of 17 June 2014 declaring certain categories of aid compatible with the internal market in application of Articles 107 and 108 of the Treaty (OJ L 187, 26.6.2014, p. 1): Article 1(3)(d); recital 12; Article 2(13); Article 1(3) final subparagraph.
- Council Decision No 2010/787/EU of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines (OJ L 336, 21.12.2010, p. 24).
- Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union: Articles 107(3)(e), 108(3).
- Council Regulation (EU) 2015/1589 laying down detailed rules for the application of Article 108 TFEU: Article 16 (recovery of unlawful aid).

8. BOTTOM LINE
No GBER exemption is available. The file must be routed to notification under Article 108(3) TFEU and assessed against Council Decision 2010/787/EU, the instrument the Regulation's scope passage (Article 1(3)(d), mirrored in recital 12) names as dealing with aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines.

question: Y138
answer:
# Legal Opinion — Derogation from ECHR Article 3 in Time of War; the Article 2 Carve-Out in Article 15(2)

**Role note.** This is written advice in the Legal Counsel function. It is a textual and doctrinal analysis of the Convention; it is not fact-specific advice on any particular State's measures, and it does not certify the validity of any actual or draft derogation notice.

---

## 1. Questions presented

1. Where a Contracting State invokes Article 15 ECHR (derogation in time of emergency) in time of war, may it derogate from Article 3 (prohibition of torture and of inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment)?
2. What narrow exception does the same non-derogation clause (Article 15 § 2) state in respect of Article 2 (right to life)?

## 2. Short answers

1. **No.** Article 15 § 2 names Article 3 among the provisions from which *no* derogation may be made under Article 15, without exception, qualification or condition. A declaration purporting to derogate from Article 3 produces no legal effect: the obligation continues in full force throughout the emergency, and the State remains answerable for every act of torture or inhuman or degrading treatment committed during it.
2. **The exception is: "deaths resulting from lawful acts of war."** Article 15 § 2 permits derogation from Article 2 *only* in respect of deaths resulting from lawful acts of war. It is an exception attached to Article 2 alone; it does not touch Article 3, Article 4 § 1 or Article 7.

## 3. Governing text

Article 15 ECHR, as published by the Registry of the European Court of Human Rights (Convention as amended; Article 15 is unamended in relevant part by Protocols Nos. 11 and 15):

> **ARTICLE 15 — Derogation in time of emergency**
>
> 1. In time of war or other public emergency threatening the life of the nation any High Contracting Party may take measures derogating from its obligations under this Convention to the extent strictly required by the exigencies of the situation, provided that such measures are not inconsistent with its other obligations under international law.
>
> 2. **No derogation from Article 2, except in respect of deaths resulting from lawful acts of war, or from Articles 3, 4 (paragraph 1) and 7 shall be made under this provision.**
>
> 3. Any High Contracting Party availing itself of this right of derogation shall keep the Secretary General of the Council of Europe fully informed of the measures which it has taken and the reasons therefor. It shall also inform the Secretary General of the Council of Europe when such measures have ceased to operate and the provisions of the Convention are again being fully executed.

The Court's own *Guide on Article 15 of the Convention – Derogation in time of emergency* (§ 38) states the effect in terms:

> "Article 15 § 2 protects certain rights from derogation. According to the text of Article 15 § 2, these are: Article 2 (the right to life), except in respect of deaths resulting from lawful acts of war; Article 3 (the prohibition of torture and other forms of ill-treatment); Article 4 § 1 (the prohibition of slavery or servitude); and Article 7 (no punishment without law)."

And the Court's *Factsheet – Derogation in time of emergency*:

> "certain Convention rights do not allow of any derogation: Article 15 § 2 thus prohibits any derogation in respect of the right to life, except in the context of lawful acts of war, the prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment …"

## 4. Analysis

### 4.1 Ask 1 — Article 3 is non-derogable; the answer is No

**(a) The prohibition is textual and unqualified.** Article 15 § 2 is drafted as a flat prohibition ("No derogation … shall be made under this provision") followed by a closed list of protected provisions. Article 3 appears in that list with **no** adverbial limitation. Contrast the treatment of Article 2 in the very same sentence, which carries the words "except in respect of deaths resulting from lawful acts of war." The drafter's choice is deliberate and dispositive: where an exception was intended, one was written; none was written for Article 3. The expressio unius reading is the only one the text supports.

**(b) Article 3 has no internal limitation clause to work with.** Article 3 is short and absolute: "No one shall be subjected to torture or to inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment." Unlike Articles 8–11 it contains no second paragraph of qualifications, and unlike Article 15 it contains no emergency gateway. Article 15 § 1 is the *only* route by which Convention obligations can be suspended in an emergency; because Article 15 § 2 closes that route for Article 3, there is no residual legal basis anywhere in the Convention for suspending Article 3. A State cannot achieve through Article 15 § 1 what Article 15 § 2 forbids, and it cannot achieve it by recharacterising the measure (e.g. as an "operational constraint" or a "temporary security measure"): the Court looks to substance, and the characterisation does not alter which Article is engaged.

**(c) The prohibition is circumstance-independent.** Because Article 15 § 2 excludes Article 3 without condition, the answer does **not** depend on whether the Article 15 § 1 threshold is met, on whether the conflict is an international or non-international armed conflict, on whether the emergency is declared, or on whether the derogation notice is procedurally perfect. If Article 15 is validly engaged, Article 3 is still non-derogable; if Article 15 is not validly engaged, the State is bound by the whole Convention and Article 3 is non-derogable. **The conclusion holds a fortiori on either branch.** This is why the verdict can be given without resolving any of the fact-dependent questions about the conflict.

**(d) A purported derogation is void, not merely reviewable.** Article 15 § 2 operates as a limit on the *right of derogation itself*, not as a defence to be weighed. A declaration purporting to derogate from Article 3 is therefore ineffective *ab initio*; it does not shift the burden, does not create a period of latitude, and does not require the Court to balance anything. Relatedly, the prohibition cannot be circumvented through a reservation: Article 57 § 1 permits reservations only to the extent they do not relate to provisions of a general character, and a reservation to Article 3 would be incompatible with the object and purpose of the Convention. Nor can it be circumvented through a Protocol: Article 3 of Protocol No. 13 (abolition of the death penalty in all circumstances) states in terms that "No derogation from the provisions of this Protocol shall be made under Article 15 of the Convention."

**(e) Reinforcing (non-essential) external anchors.** The same result follows from the State's other international obligations, which Article 15 § 1 independently requires derogating measures to respect: ICCPR Article 4 § 2 lists Article 7 (torture) among provisions from which no derogation may be made, and UNCAT Article 2 § 2 provides that "[n]o exceptional circumstances whatsoever, whether a state of war or a threat of war, internal political instability or any other public emergency, may be invoked as a justification of torture." Note carefully: the phrase "in all circumstances" is the language of ICCPR Article 4 § 2 and UNCAT, **not** of ECHR Article 15 § 2. The ECHR achieves the same effect by simple omission of any exception — the reasoning should cite the Convention text, not misquote it.

**(f) Consequence for the client.** Any measure that reaches the Article 3 threshold (torture; inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment — including, depending on intensity and duration, certain interrogation methods, conditions of detention, and ill-treatment in custody) remains a violation notwithstanding a live Article 15 derogation. The emergency is, in mitigation terms, legally irrelevant to liability under Article 3.

### 4.2 Ask 2 — The narrow Article 2 exception: "deaths resulting from lawful acts of war"

**(a) Verbatim answer.** Article 15 § 2 permits derogation from Article 2 **only** "in respect of deaths resulting from lawful acts of war." That is the whole of the exception; the clause states no other.

**(b) Why it is narrow — four cumulative limits.**

1. **It is confined to Article 2.** The exception sits inside the Article 2 limb of the sentence. It confers nothing in respect of Article 3, Article 4 § 1 or Article 7, and cannot be read across.
2. **It is confined to *deaths*.** The subject-matter is loss of life in the conduct of hostilities. It does not license detention without judicial control, denial of investigation into custody deaths, collective punishment, destruction of property, or ill-treatment — those are governed by other Articles and by Article 3's absolute prohibition.
3. **It is confined to *lawful* acts of war.** "Lawful" is a term of art pointing to the *ius in bello*: a death is within the exception only if the act causing it was lawful under international humanitarian law — e.g. directed at a military objective, observing distinction, proportionality and precautions in attack, and not directed at civilians as such. A killing that violates IHL (targeted killing of a civilian, attack on a protected object, denial of quarter, killing of a detained combatant *hors de combat*) is **not** a death resulting from a lawful act of war and falls back within Article 2's non-derogable core. This reading is reinforced by Article 15 § 1's proviso that derogating measures must not be "inconsistent with [the State's] other obligations under international law" — IHL being the paradigm case.
4. **It is a derogation, not a licence.** Even within its scope, the exception operates only "to the extent strictly required by the exigencies of the situation" (Article 15 § 1) and only subject to the Article 15 § 3 notification duty. It is not a blanket wartime immunity for lethal force.

**(c) Relationship to Article 2 § 2.** The Article 15 § 2 exception is analytically distinct from Article 2 § 2 (deprivation of life not to be regarded as inflicted in contravention of Article 2 where it results from force no more than absolutely necessary in defence, arrest or riot control). Article 2 § 2 is a *definitional* provision applicable at all times; Article 15 § 2's carve-out is a *derogation* mechanism for hostilities. In an armed-conflict setting the two are typically applied together — Article 15 § 2 supplies the derogation for combat deaths, and the Article 15 § 1 "strictly required" and international-law-consistency tests supply the discipline.

**(d) Open interpretive point (flagged, not resolved).** Whether the carve-out reaches only the substantive prohibition on deprivation of life, or also the procedural/investigative obligation read into Article 2, is not settled by the words of Article 15 § 2 alone. The safer and textually better view is that it reaches only "deaths resulting from lawful acts of war" and leaves intact the duty to account for any death outside that category. A State drafting a notice should not assume the wider reading.

**(e) Related but separate provisions (do not confuse).** Article 2 of Protocol No. 6 permits the death penalty in law "in respect of acts committed in time of war or of imminent threat of war" — a capital-punishment provision, not an Article 15 carve-out. Protocol No. 13 abolishes the death penalty in all circumstances and expressly bars derogation under Article 15. Neither alters the answer to Ask 2.

## 5. Procedural conditions attaching to any Article 15 notice (context; not part of the two answers)

- **Trigger (Art. 15 § 1):** "war or other public emergency threatening the life of the nation" — the existence of the emergency is subject to review, and the margin is wide but not unlimited.
- **Proportionality (Art. 15 § 1):** measures must be "strictly required by the exigencies of the situation" — temporally limited and revisited as the exigency abates.
- **Consistency (Art. 15 § 1):** measures must not be inconsistent with the State's other international law obligations (IHL, ICCPR, UNCAT, refugee law).
- **Notification (Art. 15 § 3):** the Secretary General of the Council of Europe must be kept fully informed of the measures taken and the reasons therefor, and informed when they cease to operate. Notification is a condition of valid derogation, and its adequacy is reviewable.
- **No derogation of the non-derogable core:** none of the above can validate a measure that touches Article 3 (or Article 4 § 1, or Article 7), and none can widen the Article 2 carve-out beyond deaths resulting from lawful acts of war.

## 6. Bottom line (operative sentences for a filing, notice or advice letter)

> Article 15 § 2 of the Convention provides that "[n]o derogation from Article 2, except in respect of deaths resulting from lawful acts of war, or from Articles 3, 4 (paragraph 1) and 7 shall be made under this provision." Article 3 is therefore non-derogable in time of war: a Contracting State invoking Article 15 may not derogate from the prohibition of torture and of inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, and any declaration or measure purporting to do so is of no legal effect. The single, narrow exception stated in the same clause concerns Article 2 alone and is limited to "deaths resulting from lawful acts of war" — that is, loss of life in the conduct of hostilities caused by acts lawful under international humanitarian law, and nothing beyond it.

## 7. Scope and limits of this opinion

- The answer rests on the primary text of Article 15 as published by the Court, corroborated by the Court's *Guide on Article 15* (§§ 1–4, 38–39) and its *Factsheet – Derogation in time of emergency*. Illustrative case law (e.g. *Lawless*, *Ireland v. the United Kingdom*, *Brannigan and McBride*, *Aksoy*, the *Greek case*) supports the surrounding Article 15 § 1/§ 3 framework but is not needed for, and does not qualify, the two answers given: no judgment of the Court has given effect to a derogation from Article 3, and the text forecloses one.
- Not assessed here: whether any particular real-world emergency satisfies Article 15 § 1; the lawfulness under IHL of any specific strike or detention; the availability of inter-State or individual applications; and the domestic constitutional route for making a derogation. Each requires its own facts.
- Where this opinion is used to draft or defend a notice, the operative constraints are the two sentences in § 6 above: **Article 3 — never derogable; Article 2 — derogable only as to deaths resulting from lawful acts of war.**

question: Y139
answer:
LEGAL NOTE — WHICH UNCITRAL TEXT THE CROSS-BORDER CONTRACTS TEAM SHOULD RETRIEVE

1. ANSWER

Retrieve the UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration (1985), with amendments as adopted in 2006.

That is the instrument whose stated scope maps one-to-one onto the four topics in the request. UNCITRAL's own description of it reads: 'It covers all stages of the arbitral process from the arbitration agreement, the composition and jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal and the extent of court intervention through to the recognition and enforcement of the arbitral award.'

Status of the text: adopted 1985 (General Assembly resolution 40/72); amended 2006 (General Assembly resolution 61/33), the amendments touching articles 1(2), 2A (new), 7, 17 (replaced by a new Chapter IV A, articles 17A-17J) and 35(2). As of 2006 the amended version is the standard version. The amended text comprises Articles 1-36 plus Article 2A and Articles 17A-17J, i.e. 47 Articles in 9 Chapters (Chapters I-VIII plus Chapter IV A).

2. WHY THIS TEXT AND NOT THE OTHER UNCITRAL CANDIDATES

- UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration (1985, as amended 2006) — CORRECT. A legislative template covering the whole arbitral lifecycle, including the four requested topics. Only instrument that covers court intervention and recognition/enforcement as a matter of the forum's own law.
- UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules (as revised in 2010, with the Expedited Arbitration Rules) — NOT the answer to this question. These are procedural rules the parties adopt for the conduct of the proceedings (appointment, pleadings, evidence, award). They presuppose a lex arbitri and say nothing about the extent of court intervention or the recognition and enforcement of awards. They remain relevant, but as the object of the clause the team drafts, not as the text answering this request.
- Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards (New York, 1958) — COMPLEMENTARY, NOT SUBSTITUTE. It covers the agreement to arbitrate (art. II) and recognition and enforcement (arts. III-V), and is the treaty that makes an award enforceable across borders. It does not regulate tribunal composition or the extent of court intervention in the seat. Retrieve it alongside, not instead.
- UNCITRAL Rules on Transparency / Mauritius Convention on Transparency (2014) — out of scope; treaty-based investor-State arbitration.
- UNCITRAL Notes on Organizing Arbitral Proceedings (2016, additional notes 2023 and 2026) and the UNCITRAL Model Clauses (SPEDR, Highly Expedited Arbitration, Adjudication, Technical Advisers, Confidentiality) — reference material for drafting, not the framework text.

3. COVERAGE MAP — THE FOUR REQUESTED TOPICS TO SPECIFIC ARTICLES (this is the answer to the scoping constraint)

(a) Arbitration agreement — Chapter II, Articles 7-9:
  - Art. 7: definition and form of the arbitration agreement (Option I; Option II is the alternative formulation retaining a writing requirement). The 2006 revision 'is intended to modernise the form required of an arbitration agreement to better conform with international contract practices.'
  - Art. 8: arbitration agreement and substantive claim before a court (court must refer parties to arbitration).
  - Art. 9: arbitration agreement and interim measures by court (request to a court for interim measures is not incompatible with the agreement).
  - Related: Art. 2 (definitions, including 'arbitration' and 'arbitral tribunal'), Art. 3 (receipt of written communications), Art. 4 (waiver of right to object).

(b) Tribunal composition and jurisdiction — Chapters III and IV:
  - Art. 10: number of arbitrators.
  - Art. 11: appointment of arbitrators (including the court/authority default appointment mechanism in 11(3)-(4)).
  - Art. 12: grounds for challenge. Art. 13: challenge procedure (13(3) — court decision on unsuccessful challenge). Art. 14: failure or impossibility to act. Art. 15: termination of mandate and substitution of arbitrator.
  - Art. 16: competence of the arbitral tribunal to rule on its own jurisdiction, including the separability presumption and the plea as to jurisdiction (16(3) — court control of a preliminary ruling upholding jurisdiction).
  - Chapter IV A (Arts. 17-17J, 2006): tribunal-ordered interim measures and preliminary orders. The 2006 revision introduced 'a more comprehensive legal regime dealing with interim measures in support of arbitration.'

(c) Court intervention — Article 5 and its cross-references:
  - Art. 5 is the chapeau rule, and the enacted text reads: 'In matters governed by this Law, no court shall intervene except where so provided in this Law.'
  - Art. 6: 'The functions referred to in articles 11(3), 11(4), 13(3), 14, 16(3) and 34(2) shall be performed by ... [Each State enacting this model law specifies the court, courts or, where referred to therein, other authority competent to perform these functions.]'
  - The closed list of permitted court functions, per the Explanatory Note, comprises two groups: (i) court assistance in taking evidence (art. 27), recognition of the arbitration agreement including its compatibility with court-ordered interim measures (arts. 8 and 9), court-ordered interim measures (art. 17J), recognition and enforcement of interim measures (arts. 17H and 17I) and of arbitral awards (arts. 35 and 36); and (ii) the supervisory functions listed in Art. 6. Beyond these, 'no court shall intervene, in matters governed by this Law' — a guarantee that 'all instances of possible court intervention are found in the piece of legislation enacting the Model Law', except matters the Model Law does not regulate (consolidation, the arbitrators' contract with parties or institution, costs and fees/deposits).
  - Also relevant on the recourse side: Art. 34 (setting aside), including the three-month time limit in Art. 34(3) and the exclusive grounds in Art. 34(2).

(d) Recognition and enforcement of the award — Chapter VIII, Articles 35-36:
  - Art. 35: recognition and enforcement; the award must be recognised as binding and enforced on application to the competent court, subject to the conditions in Arts. 35(1)-(2). Art. 35(2) is the provision amended in 2006 (and the provision addressed by the 2026 electronic-form work — see §6).
  - Art. 36: grounds for refusing recognition or enforcement, mirroring Article V of the New York Convention.
  - Related: Arts. 17H-17I (recognition and enforcement of interim measures), Art. 34 (setting aside as the exclusive recourse), Art. 2A (international origin and general principles of interpretation, 2006).

4. WHAT EXACTLY TO RETRIEVE — IDENTIFIERS AND LOCATORS

Primary:
  - Title: UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration (1985), with amendments as adopted in 2006.
  - Landing page: https://uncitral.un.org/en/texts/arbitration/modellaw/commercial_arbitration
  - Full text (UN e-book, the official English publication used as the source for this note): https://uncitral.un.org/sites/uncitral.un.org/files/media-documents/uncitral/en/07-86998_ebook.pdf
  - Explanatory Note (2008) accompanying the amended text — retrieve it with the text; it is the authoritative guide to the Chapter IV A regime and to the Art. 5 closed list.
  - Original 1985 version (retain for comparison, since many enactments are based on it): reproduced on the same landing page.

Mandatory companions:
  - Status of the Model Law (which States have enacted, and whether on the 1985 or the 2006 text): https://uncitral.un.org/en/texts/arbitration/modellaw/commercial_arbitration/status — currently 93 States in 127 jurisdictions; entries marked (b) indicate legislation based on the 2006 amended text, (a) indicates legislation amending earlier Model Law-based legislation.
  - Travaux préparatoires (for travaux-based argument on any contested article): https://uncitral.un.org/en/texts/arbitration/modellaw/commercial_arbitration/travaux
  - CLOUT abstracts and the UNCITRAL 2012 Digest of Case Law on the Model Law — for how articles 5, 7, 8, 16, 34, 35 and 36 are applied in practice.
  - New York Convention 1958 and the UNCITRAL Secretariat Guide (2016): https://uncitral.un.org/en/texts/arbitration
  - If the team's clause will adopt institutional rules: UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules (as revised in 2010) plus the 2010 Recommendations to assist arbitral institutions, and the UNCITRAL Model Clause on Highly Expedited Arbitration / Expedited Arbitration Rules if speed is a concern.
  - Language: request the six official UN language versions if the contracts are not in English; article numbering is identical across languages, so the coverage map above carries over.

5. HOW TO USE IT — FROM STATUTE TO CONTRACT PROVISIONS (important limitation)

The Model Law is a template for legislators, not a set of model contract clauses. It binds parties only to the extent a State has enacted it, and then only as the law of that State (typically the seat, and the law of the enforcing court). It therefore does two things for this team: (i) it tells them what the courts at a Model-Law seat and at a Model-Law enforcing State will do; (ii) it supplies the drafting checklist for the clause itself. The clause must still be drafted, and should be checked against:
  - Art. 7 / Art. 8: is the arbitration agreement in a form that satisfies the chosen Option, and does it cover the disputes intended (scope, pre-arbitral steps, multi-tier clauses)?
  - Art. 10 / Art. 11: is the number of arbitrators fixed, and is a default appointing authority named so that Art. 11(3)-(4) is never needed?
  - Art. 16: should the clause expressly confer jurisdiction on the tribunal to rule on its own jurisdiction, and preserve the separability of the clause?
  - Art. 5 / Art. 6: is the seat a Model-Law State, and which court performs the Art. 6 functions there? Confirm on the status page, and confirm any (a)/(b) deviations.
  - Arts. 35-36 and New York Convention arts. III-V: is the prospective enforcing State a Convention State, and has it made the reciprocity and/or commercial reservations under art. I(3)? Art. 36 of the Model Law mirrors Convention art. V, so a ground that fails under one will usually fail under the other.

6. AMENDMENT STATUS — POINT TO VERIFY BEFORE CITING

Use the 2006 amended text as the operative version. Note also, and verify before relying on it, that the Commission at its fifty-ninth session (New York, 29 June-10 July 2026) had before it draft decisions adopting revised articles of the Model Law (1985, as amended in 2006) together with corresponding revisions to the Explanatory Note, concerning arbitral awards in electronic form and the use of notices of arbitration in electronic form, with a recommendation that States consider 'the UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration, as amended in 2006 and 2026'. The revised articles are to appear in annex IV to the report of the fifty-ninth session. Until that report is confirmed as final and published, cite the 2006 text as the operative version and flag the 2026 electronic-form revision as pending; the four requested topics are unaffected in substance, since the revision concerns form (writing/electronic form) rather than the structure of court intervention or the grounds for refusal. Related and already usable: the 2006 Recommendation on the interpretation of NY Convention art. II(2) and art. VII(1) with respect to arbitral awards in electronic form.

7. QUALIFICATIONS

- The answer assumes the team wants the framework governing the arbitration (the law of the seat and of enforcement) rather than the procedural rules for running it. If the team's actual need is a clause-level text to paste into contracts, the answer to 'what to retrieve' becomes the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules (2010) model clause plus the Recommendations; the Model Law remains the framework text to check the clause against. Retrieve both if the team's need is not yet settled.
- The Model Law governs international commercial arbitration. It is not the text for investor-State arbitration (see the Mauritius Convention on Transparency and the UNCITRAL Rules on Transparency) or for purely domestic arbitration.
- Because enacting States may depart from the text, confirm the actual statute of the chosen seat and of the likely enforcing State against the status page; the UNCITRAL list is expressly indicative only.
- This note identifies and maps the text; it is not an opinion on the law of any particular seat or on the enforceability of any particular award.
