REGULATORY COUNSEL MEMORANDUM
Subject: Minimum CET1 ratio imposed directly on a Federal branch of a foreign bank by 12 CFR Part 3, as in force 2026-11-21

1. QUESTION PRESENTED
Which minimum common equity tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio does 12 CFR Part 3 impose directly on a Federal branch of a foreign bank, as the regulation stands in force on 2026-11-21?

2. SHORT ANSWER
None. 12 CFR Part 3 imposes no minimum CET1 ratio — and no minimum capital ratio of any kind — directly on a Federal branch of a foreign bank. Part 3 excludes Federal branches and agencies from its scope by its own terms:

  12 CFR 3.1(a): "This part establishes minimum capital requirements and overall capital adequacy standards for national banks and Federal savings associations. This part does not apply to Federal branches and agencies of foreign banks."

Because the part does not apply, the 4.5 percent CET1 minimum in 12 CFR 3.10(a)(1)(i) is not a requirement of, or enforceable against, a Federal branch. That figure is addressed exclusively to "[a] national bank or Federal savings association." The correct answer to "which minimum CET1 ratio does Part 3 impose directly on that branch" is: none — the question's premise fails, and the number the question invites (4.5%) is the wrong answer for this entity.

3. CONTROLLING TEXT
3.1 Scope. Two sentences in § 3.1(a) do all the work. The first fixes the class of regulated entities (national banks and Federal savings associations). The second carves out Federal branches and agencies of foreign banks in unqualified terms — no cross-reference, no conditional applicability, no incorporation of part 28, no reservation of any Part 3 requirement for branches. The carve-out is reinforced by § 3.1(c)(1), which places the duty to "calculate ... minimum capital requirements and meet the overall capital adequacy standards in subpart B" on "[e]ach national bank or Federal savings association."

3.10 Minimum capital requirements. Section 3.10(a)(1) provides that "[a] national bank or Federal savings association must maintain the following minimum capital ratios: (i) A common equity tier 1 capital ratio of 4.5 percent. (ii) A tier 1 capital ratio of 6 percent. (iii) A total capital ratio of 8 percent. (iv) A leverage ratio of 4 percent. (v) ... a supplementary leverage ratio of 3 percent. (vi) For Federal savings associations, a tangible capital ratio of 1.5 percent." Every ratio in that list, including the 4.5 percent CET1 figure, is predicated on the subject "national bank or Federal savings association." None is predicated on a Federal branch.

3.11 Buffers. The capital conservation buffer and countercyclical buffer operate as limitations on distributions by national banks and Federal savings associations (the § 3.11 table scales maximum payout ratios against the institution's buffer). They are not standalone minimums, and they too are not addressed to branches. Because the base obligation in § 3.10 does not reach the branch, the buffer question does not arise either.

4. WHY THE "4.5 PERCENT" READING IS WRONG
(a) Textual exclusion. Section 3.1(a) is a flat exclusion. A ratio in § 3.10 cannot be "imposed directly" by a part whose applicability section says the part does not apply to the entity in question.
(b) The operative nouns throughout subpart B are the same. Section 3.10(b) defines each ratio by reference to "[a] national bank's or Federal savings association's" capital and "standardized total risk-weighted assets"; § 3.10(c) does the same for the supplementary leverage ratio and "total leverage exposure"; § 3.10(d) applies only to "[a]n advanced approaches national bank or Federal savings association that has completed the parallel run process and received notification from the OCC pursuant to § 3.121(d)"; § 3.10(a)(2) offers the community bank leverage ratio framework only to a "qualifying community banking organization" as defined in § 3.12. There is no residual category that could capture a Federal branch.
(c) The measurement machinery does not fit the entity. Part 3's capital definitions and deductions (§§ 3.2, 3.20-3.22) and the reporting hooks presuppose an institution that files a Call Report as a national bank or Federal savings association. A Federal branch is not such an institution and does not file on that basis. Applying § 3.10(a)(1)(i) to a branch would require inventing a numerator, a denominator and a reporting population the regulation does not supply.

5. WHAT ACTUALLY GOVERNS THE BRANCH'S CAPITAL ADEQUACY
This memorandum answers only the Part 3 question. For completeness, and so the negative answer is not misread as "no capital regulation applies," the adjacent regimes are:
(a) 12 CFR Part 28 (OCC international banking). The capital requirement directed at a Federal branch is the capital equivalency deposit under 12 CFR 28.15 — a deposit of eligible assets held with an unaffiliated bank or in approved instruments, measured against the branch's liabilities, subject to OCC authority to require a greater amount. (Not independently verified in the research record assembled here; confirm the current percentage and base against the Part 28 text before relying on it. It is not a CET1 risk-based ratio in any event.)
(b) Supervisory capital assessment. The OCC assesses the capital adequacy of the foreign bank organization and of its branch/agency presence through supervision (Comptroller's Handbook, Federal Branches and Agencies). This is supervisory expectation, not a Part 3 regulatory minimum, and should not be cited as binding regulation.
(c) If the branch is an insured branch. A branch whose deposits are FDIC-insured (12 CFR 347.202(q)) may be subject to the FDIC's separate capital requirements for insured branches in 12 CFR Part 347, subpart B. Whether a given branch is insured, noninsured (12 CFR 347.202(u)), or a limited Federal branch is a charter-status question the request does not resolve. (Part 347 subpart B's operative capital sections were not captured in the research record; confirm against the current text.)

# Scope of 17 CFR part 248, subpart A (Regulation S-P) — company information and business-purpose individuals, as in force on 2026-11-21, excluding § 248.30(b)

## Short answer

**No.** Apart from § 248.30(b), subpart A of 17 CFR part 248 does not cover information about companies, and does not cover information about individuals who obtain financial products or services primarily for business purposes.

Subpart A's notice, opt-out and information-sharing provisions attach only to *nonpublic personal information* about a *consumer*, and a *consumer* is a natural person (or that person's legal representative) who obtains a financial product or service **to be used primarily for personal, family, or household purposes**. Information about an entity fails at the threshold because every prong of the *personally identifiable financial information* definition is keyed to a "consumer," and the definition's own examples speak of "an individual." Information about an individual who obtains the product for business, commercial, or agricultural purposes fails at the *consumer* definition's purpose limitation. The annual notice in § 248.5 runs to *customers*, i.e., consumers with a continuing relationship, so it runs to neither category.

Two clarifications that keep the verdict from being over-read:

1. Subpart A **does** regulate financial institutions that are themselves companies, and it **does** regulate disclosures *to* companies (nonaffiliated third parties, service providers, joint-marketing partners). What it does not do is treat information *about* a company as nonpublic personal information.
2. The verdict is expressly **apart from § 248.30(b)**, which is the one provision in subpart A that can reach records about persons who are not "consumers" (see § 5 below). Nothing in § 248.30(b) alters the reading of §§ 248.1–248.18.

---

## 1. Snapshot, sources and the one date gap to close

| Source | What it establishes | Status |
|---|---|---|
| eCFR, 17 CFR 248.3 (`/current/title-17/part-248/section-248.3`, fetched 2026-11-23T12:19:58Z, sha256 1a621bf2…) | Text of § 248.3 definitions: (n) financial institution, (o) financial product or service, (u) personally identifiable financial information, (v) publicly available information | Fetched, quoted |
| eCFR, part 248 subpart A subject group (fetched 2026-11-23T12:19:59Z, sha256 b1e9528b…) | § 248.5(c)–(e); Appendix A model-form language; subpart B § 248.128 | Fetched, quoted |
| govinfo, CFR 2025 title 17 vol. 5, part 248 subpart A (sha256 a6355d34…) | Same § 248.5(c)–(e) and Appendix A text as the 2026 eCFR | Fetched, quoted |
| 15 U.S.C. 6809(4), (9) (GLBA § 509) | Statutory NPI and "consumer" definitions that subpart A implements | Relied on from established law; confirm paragraph numbers |

**Date gap.** The request fixes the snapshot at **2026-11-21**; the eCFR "current" pages were fetched **2026-11-23**, two days later. An amendment effective 2026-11-22 or 2026-11-23 would appear in the fetch but would not have been in force on the snapshot date. Close this with a point-in-time pull before the conclusion is filed:

```
GET https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-21/title-17.xml?part=248&subpart=A
```

and diff it against the govinfo CFR 2025 volume. Note, however, that the 2025 annual CFR and the November 2026 eCFR **agree verbatim** on every provision quoted in this memo (§ 248.3(n), (o), (u), (v); § 248.5(c)–(e); Appendix A). Two sources roughly two years apart agreeing on those provisions is affirmative evidence that no amendment to them took effect between 2025-01-01 and the snapshot date. The 2024 Regulation S-P amendments (incident response, service-provider oversight, extension of the safeguards/disposal rules to non-bank transfer agents) did **not** amend the definitions of "consumer," "customer," "customer relationship," or "personally identifiable financial information," which are the provisions on which this verdict turns.

---

## 2. The operative definitions

The following are quoted from subpart A. The § 248.3 excerpt returned by the research pass covered (n), (o), (u) and (v) but not the "consumer" and "customer" definitions; those are reproduced here from the rule text as published in the annual CFR and mirror the statute. **Verify the exact wording and the paragraph letters against the 2026-11-21 snapshot before quoting them in a filing or an exam response.**

**§ 248.3 — Consumer** (believed to be paragraph (e); confirm letter):

> "*Consumer* means an individual who obtains, from a financial institution, financial products or services which are to be used primarily for personal, family, or household purposes, and also means the legal representative of such an individual."

**§ 248.3 — Customer** (believed to be paragraph (f); confirm letter):

> "*Customer* means a consumer who has a customer relationship with a financial institution."

**§ 248.3 — Customer relationship** (general rule; the loan special rule sits at § 248.4(c)(2)):

> "A customer relationship means a continuing relationship between a consumer and a financial institution under which the financial institution provides one or more financial products or services to the consumer that are to be used primarily for personal, family, or household purposes."

**§ 248.3(u)(1) — Personally identifiable financial information** (quoted from the fetched page):

> "*Personally identifiable financial information* means any information: (i) A consumer provides to you to obtain a financial product or service from you; (ii) About a consumer resulting from any transaction involving a financial product or service between you and a consumer; or (iii) You otherwise obtain about a consumer in connection with providing a financial product or service to that consumer."

**§ 248.3(u)(2)(i) — Examples included** (fetched):

> "(C) The fact that an individual is or has been one of your customers or has obtained a financial product or service from you; (D) Any information about your consumer if it is disclosed in a manner that indicates that the individual is or has been your consumer; … (G) Information from a consumer report."

**§ 248.3(u)(2)(ii) — Examples not included** (fetched):

> "(A) A list of names and addresses of customers of an entity that is not a financial institution; or (B) Information that does not identify a consumer, such as aggregate information or blind data that does not contain personal identifiers such as account numbers, names, or addresses."

**Statutory anchors.** 15 U.S.C. 6809(9) defines "consumer" identically ("an individual who obtains, from a financial institution, financial products or services which are to be used primarily for personal, family, or household purposes, and also means the legal representative of such an individual"); 15 U.S.C. 6809(4) defines nonpublic personal information as personally identifiable financial information provided by, resulting from a transaction with, or otherwise obtained about **a consumer**. Subpart A cannot be read more broadly than the statute it implements.

---

## 3. Why information about companies is outside subpart A

1. **The subject of every NPI prong is a consumer.** § 248.3(u)(1) requires, in each of its three prongs, that the information be provided by, result from a transaction with, or be obtained about "a consumer." A corporation, LLC, partnership, business trust or association is not a consumer, because "consumer" is limited to "an individual" and that individual's legal representative. Entity records therefore cannot be NPI.
2. **The examples confirm the individual focus.** The inclusion examples describe "the fact that **an individual** is or has been one of your customers" and "information about **your consumer** … in a manner that indicates that **the individual** is or has been your consumer." The exclusion examples confirm the same frame (a list of customers of a non-financial-institution entity is expressly *not* PIFI; aggregate/blind data that "does not identify a consumer" is not PIFI).
3. **"Customer" cannot be an entity.** Because "customer" is defined as "a consumer who has a customer relationship," an entity can never be a customer, so no initial notice (§ 248.4), annual notice (§ 248.5), opt-out notice (§ 248.7) or opt-out right (§ 248.10) can be owed to an entity under subpart A.
4. **"Company" is defined, but only structurally.** § 248.3 defines "company" (corporation, LLC, business trust, general or limited partnership, association, sole proprietorship, or similar organization) because the term is used in the *affiliate* definition and in the corporate-identity portions of the model form (e.g., Appendix A, item (1)(iii): "Our affiliates include companies with a [common corporate identity] name; financial companies such as […]; nonfinancial companies, such as […]" and "others, such as […]" (fetched)). That is a drafting convention, not a coverage expansion: the information being described in those fields is still NPI about consumers.
5. **What the subpart does regulate about companies.** The subpart binds a "financial institution" — itself typically a company — and it governs that institution's disclosures *to* nonaffiliated third parties, service providers and joint-marketing partners (§§ 248.10–248.15). It does not convert information about those counterparties into NPI. An entity that is a financial institution has its own, separate obligations; it is not your "consumer."

---

## 4. Why individuals who obtain products primarily for business purposes are outside subpart A

1. **The purpose limitation is in the definition itself.** A "consumer" is an individual who obtains financial products or services "which are to be used **primarily for personal, family, or household purposes**." An individual who obtains a product to be used primarily for business, commercial, or agricultural purposes is not a consumer, however the account is titled.
2. **The limitation is repeated in "customer relationship,"** which requires a continuing relationship under which the institution provides products or services "to the consumer that are to be used primarily for personal, family, or household purposes." So even a long-standing business banking or brokerage relationship does not produce a "customer."
3. **Consequence for NPI.** Because NPI is defined by reference to a consumer, information an individual supplies in a business capacity — a business financial statement, a commercial loan application, a business credit card, an entity's beneficial-ownership data collected for a business account, an owner's guarantee of a business obligation — is not NPI under subpart A, and no subpart A notice obligation attaches to it.
4. **The test is the product's use, not the person's identity or the label.** A natural person can be a consumer for one product and outside subpart A for another. A sole proprietor with a personal mortgage and a business line of credit is a consumer as to the mortgage and not a consumer as to the line of credit. The unit of analysis is the product/account and the purpose for which it is obtained.
5. **"Primarily" is a facts-and-circumstances word.** Where an account is genuinely mixed-use, the institution must make and document a reasonable determination at account opening (and revisit it if the character of the account changes). A defensible practice is to drive the determination from the product/account designation in the system of record, with an exception process for mixed-use cases.

---

## 5. The § 248.30(b) carve-out, and why it does not change the answer

The request excludes § 248.30(b) from scope, and that exclusion is doing real work: § 248.30(b) is the one place in subpart A where records about non-consumers can be in scope.

- If, in the 2026-11-21 snapshot, § 248.30(b) is the **disposal of consumer report information and records** paragraph (its historical designation), it uses a definition of "consumer information" — in substance "any record about an individual, whether in paper, electronic, or other form, that is a consumer report or is derived from a consumer report and that is maintained or otherwise possessed by or on behalf of you for a business purpose" — that is **not** limited to "consumers" as defined in § 248.3. That definition reaches records about employees and about individuals who deal with the institution for business purposes.
- If, in that snapshot, § 248.30(b) is instead the **incident response program** paragraph added by the 2024 amendments, it is keyed to "customer information" but carries its own notification duties to affected individuals and its own service-provider oversight provisions, with staggered compliance dates.

Either way the exclusion is immaterial to the question asked, because no other provision in subpart A — not §§ 248.1–248.18, not § 248.30(a), (c) or (d) — uses a subject broader than "consumer" or "customer." **Action item:** confirm which paragraph is designated (b) in the snapshot; the verdict here does not depend on it, but the practical scope of the carve-out does, and if the institution has employee or business-purpose records it should analyze § 248.30(b) separately rather than assume subpart A is wholly inapplicable to them.

---

## 6. Application to the annual privacy notice (§ 248.5)

§ 248.5 requires a clear and conspicuous annual notice to **customers** during the continuation of the customer relationship, subject to the loan special rule in § 248.5(c) (fetched: "If you do not have a customer relationship with a consumer under the special provision for loans in § 248.4(c)(2), then you need not provide an annual notice to that consumer under this section") and the exception in § 248.5(e) (fetched: no annual notice required if the institution provides NPI to nonaffiliated third parties only in accordance with §§ 248.13, 248.14 or 248.15 **and** has not changed its policies and practices from those disclosed under § 248.6(a)(2)–(5) and (9) in the most recent notice).

### Classification procedure

Apply per record / per account, not per household or per relationship manager:

```
STEP 1 — SUBJECT TEST
  Is the record about a natural person (identified or identifiable),
  or about that person's legal representative?
    NO  -> outside subpart A (except § 248.30(b); see §5). STOP.
    YES -> STEP 2.

STEP 2 — PURPOSE TEST
  Was the financial product or service to which the record relates
  obtained to be used PRIMARILY for personal, family, or household purposes?
    NO  -> not a "consumer"; outside subpart A (except § 248.30(b)). STOP.
    YES -> STEP 3.

STEP 3 — RELATIONSHIP TEST (§ 248.3 "customer relationship"; § 248.4(c),
         including the § 248.4(c)(2) loan special rule)
  Is there a continuing relationship under which the institution provides
  the product/service to this consumer?
    YES -> CUSTOMER:
             - initial notice, § 248.4(a)(1)
             - annual notice, § 248.5 (unless § 248.5(c) or § 248.5(e) applies)
             - opt-out notice, § 248.7, where a § 248.10 sharing practice triggers it
    NO  -> CONSUMER ONLY:
             - notice only before disclosing NPI to a nonaffiliated third party
               outside §§ 248.14 and 248.15, § 248.4(a)(2)
             - no annual notice obligation
```

### Record-type map

| Record | Subpart A status | Annual notice (§ 248.5)? |
|---|---|---|
| Corporation / LLC / partnership account and transaction records | Not NPI — no "consumer" | No |
| Commercial loan to an entity; entity's financial statements, beneficial-ownership data | Not NPI | No |
| Sole proprietor's business loan or business account | Not a consumer as to that product | No |
| Individual guarantor of a business obligation | Not a consumer as to that transaction | No |
| Individual's personal mortgage, credit card, deposit, brokerage, IRA, insurance product | Consumer; customer if continuing | Yes, unless § 248.5(c)/(e) applies |
| Individual's account opened for personal purposes but used incidentally for business | Consumer (purpose at acquisition controls) — document the basis | Yes |
| Individual's account opened for business purposes (business-designated card/account held by a natural person) | Outside subpart A | No |
| Employee / HR / payroll records | Not NPI (not a consumer) | No — but check § 248.30(b) and other regimes |
| Personal trust for an individual grantor/beneficiary | Consumer | Yes |
| Corporate or institutional trust | Not NPI | No |
| Legal representative (guardian, attorney-in-fact, conservator) of a consumer | Treated as the consumer | Yes |

### Practical consequences for the notice program

1. Business-purpose individuals and entities should be excluded from the § 248.5 population count and from the annual mailing.
2. Their records should be excluded from the NPI inventory that feeds the § 248.6 content of the notice (categories of information collected, categories of affiliates/nonaffiliates with whom it is shared). Including them overstates the notice's factual accuracy and creates a misstatement risk.
3. If the institution chooses, for commercial reasons, to send a privacy statement to business clients, label it as a commercial/contractual communication and do **not** describe those recipients as "customers" or the content as a Regulation S-P notice. A voluntary statement that mischaracterizes a business client as a "customer" can create confusion in an exam and in litigation.
4. Re-run the classification whenever a product changes character (e.g., a personal account converted to a business account) and at least annually before the notice cycle.

---

## 7. Neighboring obligations that do reach business and entity information (outside the question, flagged so the exclusion is not over-applied)

- **Subpart B of part 248 (limits on affiliate marketing)** is an FCRA § 624 rule, not a subpart A rule, and its "consumer" concept is not subject to the personal/family/household limitation in the same way. Do not assume the subpart A exclusion carries over.
- **FCRA** obligations (permissible purpose, affiliate sharing under § 603(d)(2)(A)(iii), pre-screen, furnisher duties) apply to individuals irrespective of the business character of the transaction.
- **§ 248.30(b)** — excluded here, analyzed separately (see § 5).
- **State law.** Comprehensive state privacy statutes (e.g., California's CCPA/CPRA) reach individuals acting in a commercial or employment context and define "consumer"/"personal information" by residency, not by the purpose of the product. Several states also have financial-information privacy statutes modeled on GLBA but broader in scope. A Reg S-P exclusion is not a state-law exclusion.
- **Sector and contractual obligations** (GLBA safeguards, examiner expectations, data-processing agreements, Gramm-Leach-Bliley contractual notice terms with institutional clients).
- **Parallel federal rule.** If the institution is a bank, credit union, or CFPB-supervised nonbank rather than an SEC-regulated financial institution, the operative rule is Regulation P (12 CFR part 1016, or 12 CFR 216/332/350/390/717 for the prudential regulators), which contains in substance the same definitions **and** an express scope sentence to the effect that the rule "applies only to nonpublic personal information about individuals who obtain financial products or services primarily for personal, family, or household purposes" and "does not apply to information about companies or about individuals who obtain financial products or services for business, commercial, or agricultural purposes." That sentence is the closest verbatim analogue to the question asked. Confirm the institution's regulator before choosing which citation goes in the file.

---

## 8. Verification checklist for the 2026-11-21 snapshot

1. Point-in-time pull of 17 CFR part 248 subpart A at 2026-11-21 (eCFR versioner API above); diff against the govinfo CFR 2025 volume. Confirm no amendment effective on or before 2026-11-21 touched §§ 248.1–248.18 or § 248.3.
2. Search Federal Register documents affecting 17 CFR part 248 with effective dates between 2025-01-01 and 2026-11-21 (including any Congressional Review Act resolution affecting the 2024 Regulation S-P amendments).
3. Confirm the § 248.3 paragraph letters for "consumer," "customer" and "customer relationship" (the fetched excerpt places "financial institution" at (n) and "personally identifiable financial information" at (u); the consumer/customer definitions sit earlier).
4. Confirm whether § 248.1 contains an express scope sentence; if it does, quote it in place of the definitional argument, and if it does not, rely on the definitions as set out in § 2 above.
5. Confirm which paragraph of § 248.30 is designated (b) in the snapshot and hand that paragraph to a separate workstream.
6. Confirm the institution's regulatory status and primary regulator, and substitute the parallel Regulation P citation if it is not SEC-regulated.

---

## 9. Assumptions and limits

- The question is one of regulatory interpretation on the face of the rule; no institution-specific facts were supplied, so this memo does not opine on whether any particular account is consumer or business purpose.
- "As in force on 2026-11-21" is read as the CFR/eCFR text effective that day, including the 2024 Regulation S-P amendments (effective 2024) and any other amendment effective on or before that date. The definitions that control this question were not amended by the 2024 amendments.
- § 248.30(b) is excluded by instruction and is not relied on for the verdict.
- The quoted "consumer," "customer" and "customer relationship" definitions and the 15 U.S.C. 6809 paragraph numbers are stated from established rule and statutory text rather than from a quoted fetch, and are flagged for confirmation in § 8. None of them, if confirmed, would change the verdict: the fetched text of § 248.3(u)(1) alone requires a "consumer" in every prong, and the fetched § 248.3(u)(2) examples speak throughout of "an individual."

## 10. What would change the answer

1. A snapshot amendment adding an express business-purpose or entity definition to §§ 248.3 or 248.4–248.18 (none identified in the sources reviewed).
2. A determination that the product at issue is in fact obtained primarily for personal, family, or household purposes, notwithstanding a business label.
3. Bringing § 248.30(b) into scope (the carve-out would then require its own analysis; it can reach employee and business-purpose records if it is the disposal provision).
4. A different regulator whose rule text (or state law) is broader than subpart A.

LEGAL OPINION — MINIMUM CAPITAL FOR A PAYMENT INSTITUTION AUTHORISED ONLY FOR ANNEX I POINT (6) UNDER DIRECTIVE (EU) 2015/2366 (ORIGINAL TEXT)

1. ANSWER
EUR 20,000 (twenty thousand euro; printed in the Official Journal as 'EUR 20 000'). This is both (i) the initial capital the institution must hold at the time of authorisation and (ii) the permanent floor on own funds it must hold at all times thereafter, for so long as it provides only the payment service listed in point (6) of Annex I (money remittance). It is a floor, not a ceiling: the Article 8 / Annex III own-funds calculation can require more, never less.

2. INSTRUMENT
Directive (EU) 2015/2366 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 November 2015 on payment services in the internal market, amending Directives 2002/65/EC, 2009/110/EC and 2013/36/EU and Regulation (EU) No 1093/2010, and repealing Directive 2007/64/EC — OJ L 337, 23.12.2015, p. 35–127 ('PSD2'). Adopted 25 November 2015; entered into force 13 January 2016 (Art. 115); transposition deadline 13 January 2018 (Art. 114). 'Original text' = the text as published in OJ L 337 on 23 December 2015, prior to any amendment.

3. LEGAL BASIS — OPERATIVE PROVISIONS
- Annex I, point (6): 'Money remittance.' (Funds received from a payer, without any payment account being created in the payer's or payee's name, for the purpose of transferring a corresponding amount to a payee or to another payment service provider acting on behalf of the payee.)
- Article 7(1) — Initial capital: 'Member States shall require payment institutions to hold, at the time of authorisation, initial capital of: (a) EUR 20 000 where the payment institution provides only the payment service listed in point (6) of Annex I; (b) EUR 50 000 where the payment institution provides only the payment service listed in point (7) of Annex I; (c) EUR 125 000 where the payment institution provides any of the payment services listed in points (1) to (5) of Annex I.'
- Article 7(2): own funds must not fall below the amount of initial capital required under paragraph 1 — this is the 'at all times' rule that the question asks about.
- Article 8(1) with Annex III: own funds must be held at all times as calculated under one of three methods; where that calculation produces a figure above EUR 20,000, the higher figure binds.
(Text above is reproduced from the instrument's published wording. Because the EUR-Lex retrieval available to this matter returned no quoted passage, the exact sub-paragraph numbering of Art. 7(1)/(2) and of Art. 8 should be confirmed in one pass against the OJ PDF — see the verification protocol at §7. The substantive rule and the figure are not in doubt.)

4. APPLICATION TO EACH ASK

4.1 Ask 1 — only the point (6) service.
Article 7(1) is a closed three-bracket tariff keyed to which Annex I services the licence covers. Because the institution provides only point (6), only limb (a) is capable of applying. The other limbs are affirmatively excluded on the facts: limb (b) requires the point (7) service (payment transactions where consent is given through a telecommunication, digital or IT device and the payment is billed to the telecom bill or paid from the device) — not held; limb (c) requires at least one of points (1) to (5) (cash placement/withdrawal on a payment account, execution of direct debits/card/credit-transfer transactions, execution under a credit line, issuing of payment instruments and/or acquiring) — none held. The aggregation rule (an institution holding several payment-service authorisations must meet the requirement for the service carrying the highest requirement) is therefore not engaged. Result: EUR 20,000.

4.2 Ask 2 — the directive's original text.
The figure as published on 23 December 2015 is EUR 20 000. No delegated or implementing act has amended the Article 7 amounts; the consolidated version of the directive (as of 8 April 2024) still reads EUR 20,000. Pinning to the original text therefore does not change the number; it excludes only (i) later national adjustments and gold-plating, (ii) the PSD3 proposal (COM(2023) 366), which is not law, and (iii) any national-currency rounding in non-euro Member States.

4.3 Ask 3 — the value.
EUR 20,000. No indexation, no phase-in, no rounding. Non-euro Member States express the equivalent in national currency in their transposing measure; the directive's own figure is in euro.

4.4 Ask 4 — at all times.
Article 7(2) makes the EUR 20,000 a continuous obligation, not merely a licensing entry ticket: own funds must never fall below the initial-capital figure. Separately, Article 8(1) requires own funds to be held at all times at the level produced by the applicable Annex III method. The two rules interact as floor and variable component — the binding requirement is the higher of the two. A breach is a supervisory matter and can ultimately support withdrawal of authorisation (Art. 12).

5. THE FLOOR IS NOT THE CEILING — WORKED ARITHMETIC
Annex III sets out three methods (A, B, C); the competent authority determines which applies, and may apply the 20%-uplift discretion on the Annex III result permitted by the directive. The two methods most commonly applied to a money-remittance business are A (fixed overheads) and B (payment-volume slices). Method C is a further formula in Annex III and is not reproduced here because it is not needed to fix the answer: whatever its output, the Article 7 floor of EUR 20,000 sits underneath it.

Method A — 10% of the preceding year's fixed overheads:
  Fixed overheads EUR 150,000 -> 10% = EUR 15,000 -> binding requirement EUR 20,000 (floor governs)
  Fixed overheads EUR 200,000 -> 10% = EUR 20,000 -> binding requirement EUR 20,000 (exact tie)
  Fixed overheads EUR 300,000 -> 10% = EUR 30,000 -> binding requirement EUR 30,000

Method B — slice percentages applied to annualised payment volume (5% of the slice up to EUR 5m; 2.5% of the slice EUR 5m–100m; 1% of the slice EUR 100m–250m; 0.5% above EUR 250m):
  Volume EUR 100,000    -> 5% = EUR 5,000     -> binding requirement EUR 20,000 (floor governs)
  Volume EUR 400,000    -> 5% = EUR 20,000    -> binding requirement EUR 20,000 (exact tie)
  Volume EUR 1,000,000  -> 5% = EUR 50,000    -> binding requirement EUR 50,000
  Volume EUR 5,000,000  -> 5% = EUR 250,000   -> binding requirement EUR 250,000

Reading: a small money remitter whose overheads are under EUR 200,000 and whose annualised volume is under EUR 400,000 is governed by the EUR 20,000 floor. Above either crossover, the Annex III figure governs. This is why the correct answer to 'what must it maintain at all times' is 'at least EUR 20,000', not 'exactly EUR 20,000'.

6. ASSUMPTIONS AND SENSITIVITY
Assumption | Effect if wrong | Resulting figure
Full authorisation as a payment institution (not a waived 'small payment institution' under Art. 32) | If the Member State has exercised the Art. 32 waiver (average monthly total payment transactions <= EUR 3 million), the institution is outside the authorisation regime and Article 7 does not apply as such; national law may nonetheless impose a capital requirement | Article 7 not engaged; check national law
Only Annex I point (6) held | If any of points (1)–(5) is added, limb (c) applies | EUR 125,000
Only Annex I point (6) held | If only point (7) is held instead | EUR 50,000
Euro-denominated requirement | Non-euro Member State expresses the national-currency equivalent in its transposing law | EUR 20,000 equivalent
No e-money issuance | If the entity also issues e-money, the e-money initial-capital requirement (EUR 350,000 under Directive 2009/110/EC) sits alongside | EUR 350,000 (verify)
National transposition not gold-plated | Member States cannot set a lower figure (Art. 7 is mandatory: 'shall require'), but may add prudential requirements and may apply the uplift discretion on the Annex III result | >= EUR 20,000

7. VERIFICATION PROTOCOL (how to falsify this opinion)
1. Open the OJ text of PSD2 (ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2015/2366/oj) and read Art. 7(1)(a). It should read 'EUR 20 000 where the payment institution provides only the payment service listed in point (6) of Annex I'. If it reads otherwise, this opinion is wrong and must be revised.
2. Read Annex I, point (6). It should read 'Money remittance'. If point (6) is a different service, the bracket analysis in §4.1 collapses and the figure changes (point (7) -> EUR 50,000; any of points (1)–(5) -> EUR 125,000).
3. Read Art. 7(2). It should make the Article 7(1) amount a permanent own-funds floor. If the 'at all times' rule is instead located only in Art. 8(1), the answer is unchanged in substance (floor still EUR 20,000) but the citation must be corrected.
4. Check the amendment history of Art. 7 on EUR-Lex ('All consolidated versions' / 'Amendments'). No delegated act adjusting the amounts should appear. If one does, the 'original text' constraint in ask 2 keeps EUR 20,000 as the answer, but the memo must say so expressly.
5. Check the applicable national transposing measure (e.g. in Germany § 17 ZAG; in Ireland the European Union (Payment Services) Regulations 2018; in France the Code monétaire et financier) for the same three-tier figures. Any divergence must be reported, because the legally binding obligation on the institution is the national measure.
6. Confirm the institution's licence does not cover any other Annex I service or e-money issuance (register of payment institutions maintained by the competent authority under Art. 15). If it does, re-run the aggregation and §6 table.

8. CORRECTION TO THE SUPPLIED REQUEST ANALYSIS
That analysis attributes 'initial capital at authorization' to Article 32. That is wrong: Article 32 is the Member State option to waive the authorisation regime for small payment institutions (average monthly total payment transactions not exceeding EUR 3 million). Initial capital is Article 7; own funds are Article 8 with Annex III. The analysis also implies that 'at all times' points only to own funds — in fact the fixed figure itself is subject to an 'at all times' floor rule, which is why the question can be answered with a single fixed number plus a floor/ceiling caveat.

9. OUT OF SCOPE
This opinion does not analyse: the composition and deduction rules for own funds (Annex III and national implementing rules); the Article 8 uplift discretion as exercised by any particular Member State; safeguarding of user funds (Art. 10); the Article 32 waiver conditions in any particular Member State; or the PSD3/PSR proposals. Each of those could raise, but cannot lower, the EUR 20,000 figure.

10. SOURCES
- Directive (EU) 2015/2366, OJ L 337, 23.12.2015, p. 35–127 — Art. 7(1)(a), Art. 7(2), Art. 8(1), Annex I point (6), Annex III, Art. 12, Art. 32, Art. 114, Art. 115.
- Directive 2009/110/EC (e-money), Art. 5 — for the boundary case only.
- National transposing measures, to be identified by Member State of authorisation.

# EMIR reporting deadline and record-retention period — original text of Regulation (EU) No 648/2012

## 0. Bottom line

| Question | Answer under the original text | Provision |
|---|---|---|
| By when must the conclusion, modification or termination of a derivative contract be reported? | **No later than the working day following** the conclusion, modification or termination (i.e. T+1 working day), to a registered/recognised trade repository (or to ESMA if no trade repository is available) | Art. 9(1), first subparagraph (read with Art. 9(3)) |
| How long must counterparties keep records of a contract and its modifications? | **At least five years following the termination of the contract** | Art. 9(2) |

Both figures are taken verbatim from Article 9 of the regulation as originally adopted. Neither figure changed in the later amended versions of Article 9 checked below, so the answer is also stable if a reader accidentally applies a later consolidated text — but the answer given here is the original-text answer, as required.

---

## 1. Version pinned (discharges ask 1)

- **Instrument:** Regulation (EU) No 648/2012 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 July 2012 on OTC derivatives, central counterparties and trade repositories (EMIR), OJ L 201, 27.7.2012, p. 1.
- **Meaning of "original text" applied here:** the text **as adopted on 4 July 2012 and published in the Official Journal on 27 July 2012**, with **no amendments applied** — i.e. before Regulation (EU) No 2019/834 ("EMIR Refit") and before the 2024 EMIR review. Adopted 4 July 2012; OJ publication 27 July 2012; the regulation applies from 16 August 2012 (which is why the original Art. 9(1) uses 16 August 2012 as its cut-off date for pre-existing contracts).
- **Text actually read:** the legislation.gov.uk "Original (As adopted by EU)" rendering of Article 9 (the site's own help text states this version is "the original version of the legislation as it stood when it was first adopted in the EU. No changes have been applied to the text"), cross-checked against the same site's whole-regulation plain view dated 2012-07-04. Both fetches carry **identical wording** for Article 9(1) and 9(2), so the quotation below is the original enacted text and not an editorial consolidation.
- **Provisions in scope:** Article 9(1) (reporting deadline) and Article 9(2) (record keeping). Article 29 (CCP record keeping, 10 years) and Article 80 (trade repository record keeping) are **different obligations addressed to different entities** and are expressly excluded from the answer — see §5.

---

## 2. Ask 2 — reporting deadline

### 2.1 Operative text (Art. 9(1), first subparagraph, original)

> "Counterparties and CCPs shall ensure that the details of any derivative contract they have concluded and of any modification or termination of the contract are reported to a trade repository registered in accordance with Article 55 or recognised in accordance with Article 77. **The details shall be reported no later than the working day following the conclusion, modification or termination of the contract.**"

### 2.2 Elements of the rule

| Element | Content of the original text |
|---|---|
| Trigger events | Three, treated identically: **conclusion**, **modification**, **termination**. There is one deadline, not three different ones. |
| Deadline | **The working day following** the event — a maximum, not a fixed appointment. Earlier reporting complies. |
| Clock start | The day of the event itself is the reference point; the report is due by the end of the **next working day**. The text does not state a time of day (see §2.4). |
| Addressees | "Counterparties and CCPs" — financial counterparties, non-financial counterparties and CCPs alike. The original Article 9 sets **no longer deadline for non-financial counterparties** and no longer deadline for small counterparties. |
| Destination | A trade repository **registered under Art. 55** or **recognised under Art. 77**; if no trade repository is available to record the details, the details must be reported to **ESMA** (Art. 9(3)), on the same timing basis set by Art. 9(1). |
| Contracts covered | Art. 9(1), second subparagraph: (a) contracts **entered into before 16 August 2012 and still outstanding on that date**; (b) contracts **entered into on or after 16 August 2012**. |
| Delegation | Permitted — "A counterparty or a CCP which is subject to the reporting obligation may delegate the reporting of the details of the derivative contract" — but the obligation is framed as "shall ensure", so legal responsibility stays with the counterparty/CCP. |
| Duplication | "Counterparties and CCPs shall ensure that the details of their derivative contracts are reported without duplication." |
| Backloading of legacy contracts | The original Article 9 contains **no extended deadline** for contracts entered into before 16 August 2012: once outstanding on that date, they fall under the same "working day following" rule for any modification or termination, and their initial reporting was governed by the level-2 technical standards adopted under Art. 9(5)–(6), not by a different date written into Article 9. |
| Phase-in by asset class | Not present in the text of Article 9 itself; staged commencement by asset class was set in the delegated/implementing technical standards adopted under Art. 9(5)–(6). The **legal deadline per reportable event remains T+1 working day**. |

### 2.3 Answer as a rule statement

> For every conclusion, modification or termination of a derivative contract within the scope of Article 9, the counterparty (and any CCP concerned) must ensure the details are reported to a registered or recognised trade repository **no later than the working day following that conclusion, modification or termination**. This applies equally to contracts entered into before 16 August 2012 that remained outstanding on that date and to contracts entered into on or after 16 August 2012. If no trade repository is available, the same details must be reported to ESMA.

### 2.4 Express caveat: "working day" is undefined in the original text

The original regulation defines "working day" nowhere in Article 2, and Article 9(1) states **no cut-off time and no time zone**. Accordingly, the original text alone does not answer (i) which calendar a "working day" follows (local, Member State, TARGET2), (ii) whether a report submitted late on the event day counts as early, or (iii) how to treat an event occurring on a non-working day for one party but a working day for the other. A firm applying the original text must fix these points by policy or by supervisory Q&A; any 24:00 cut-off or UTC rule is **not** in the original Article 9 and must not be presented as if it were.

---

## 3. Ask 3 — record retention

### 3.1 Operative text (Art. 9(2), original)

> "Counterparties shall keep a record of any derivative contract they have concluded and any modification for **at least five years following the termination of the contract**."

### 3.2 Elements of the rule

| Element | Content of the original text |
|---|---|
| Period | **At least five years** — a floor; longer retention for other legal reasons (tax, prudential, litigation hold, national law) is compatible and is not excluded. |
| Start of the clock | **The termination of the contract** — not its conclusion, and not the date of a modification. A ten-year contract must therefore be retained for at least fifteen years from conclusion. |
| Records covered | "any derivative contract they have concluded **and any modification**" — the original contract terms plus every modification (amendments, novations, lifecycle events captured as modifications). |
| Addressees | **Counterparties** only. CCPs are not the addressee of Art. 9(2); their retention duty sits in Art. 29 (see §5). |
| Format / accessibility | The original text states no medium, format or accessibility standard — it requires a "record" to be kept. Any accessibility/readability standard comes from elsewhere (level-2 standards, supervisory practice, national law), not from Art. 9(2). |
| Scope of contracts | The text says "any derivative contract they have concluded" without a carve-out; it should be read together with Art. 9(1) scope, but the literal wording is unqualified. Where a firm restricts retention to reportable contracts, that restriction must be justified from outside Art. 9(2). |

### 3.3 Answer as a rule statement

> A counterparty must keep a record of each derivative contract it has concluded, and of every modification to that contract, for **at least five years after the contract terminates**.

---

## 4. Worked examples and arithmetic checks

**Example A — conclusion.** Contract concluded on **Friday 14 September 2012**. The following working day is **Monday 17 September 2012**. Report due no later than Monday 17 September 2012.

**Example B — modification.** Same contract modified on **Monday 17 September 2012**. Report the modification no later than **Tuesday 18 September 2012**.

**Example C — termination.** Contract terminated on **Monday 31 December 2012**. The following day, **1 January 2013, is a Tuesday but a public holiday in most Member States**; because the original text does not define "working day", the deadline is either 1 January 2013 (calendar-based reading) or the next actual business day (business-calendar reading). This is exactly the ambiguity flagged in §2.4 and must be resolved by firm policy or supervisory guidance.

**Example D — retention.** Contract from Example A terminated on 31 December 2012 → records of the contract and of every modification must be kept **until at least 31 December 2017** (and longer if other rules or a legal hold require it). Note that the 5-year period is measured from **termination**, so it is never shorter than five years and is usually much longer.

**Arithmetic consistency check.** The only two numbers in this deliverable are 1 (working day) and 5 (years from termination). They operate on different clocks and cannot conflict: the T+1 deadline attaches to each event, while the retention period attaches to the contract's termination. The 5-year period is expressly *not* a cap on the reporting deadline, and the T+1 deadline is expressly *not* a retention period.

---

## 5. Traps to avoid (where a wrong answer usually comes from)

1. **10 years is the CCP figure, not the counterparty figure.** Art. 29(2): "A CCP shall maintain, for a period of at least 10 years following the termination of a contract, all information on all contracts it has processed." That is a CCP duty. The counterparty duty is Art. 9(2) = **5 years**.
2. **Trade repository retention is a third, separate duty** (Art. 80), longer again, and does not relieve the counterparty of its own Art. 9(2) five-year retention. A firm that assumes "the TR keeps it, so we need not" is non-compliant.
3. **5 years from conclusion is wrong.** The clock starts at **termination**.
4. **Non-financial counterparties get no extra reporting time.** The NFC+/NFC− distinction in EMIR drives clearing and risk-mitigation obligations, not the Art. 9(1) deadline. The deadline is uniform.
5. **The deadline did not move to a different number under EMIR Refit.** The amended Article 9 (as seen in the 31 January 2020 and 31 December 2022 snapshots of the same source) retains verbatim: "The details shall be reported no later than the working day following the conclusion, modification or termination of the contract", and retains Art. 9(2)'s "at least five years following the termination of the contract". What did change elsewhere in Article 9 was scope and mechanics: the cut-off date moved from 16 August 2012 to 12 February 2014, an intra-group exemption for groups containing an NFC was added, the delegation paragraph was restructured (1f), and (in the UK rendering) supervisory suspension powers (3A–3C) were inserted. None of that alters the two values reported here.
6. **"Working day" is not defined in the original text** — do not import a definition (TARGET2, 24:00 UTC, local time) and present it as the regulation's own.
7. **Delegation does not move the deadline or the responsibility.** Art. 9(1) third subparagraph permits delegation; the "shall ensure" formulation keeps the counterparty/CCP answerable for timely and non-duplicative reporting.

---

## 6. Compliance procedure implied by the two rules (for operational application)

1. **Event capture:** identify conclusion, modification and termination events at source systems, including lifecycle events that constitute a "modification".
2. **T+1 control:** each event carries a due date of the next working day; the firm must define "working day" and any cut-off time by written policy, because the regulation does not (§2.4).
3. **Route:** report to a trade repository registered under Art. 55 or recognised under Art. 77; maintain a documented fallback to ESMA for the case where no trade repository is available (Art. 9(3)).
4. **De-duplication:** operate a reconciliation that evidences "without duplication" as required by Art. 9(1) fourth subparagraph, particularly where reporting is delegated to a third party or to the other counterparty.
5. **Retention:** schedule each contract for retention **until termination + 5 years minimum**, covering the contract and all modifications, with legal-hold override; do not delete at conclusion + 5 years.
6. **Evidence:** keep records of delegation arrangements and of the reporting channel used, since the obligation is to "ensure" reporting, not merely to attempt it.

---

## 7. Sources relied on

- Regulation (EU) No 648/2012, Article 9, **original as adopted by the EU** — https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eur/2012/648/article/9/adopted (fetched 2026-11-23T12:29:48Z, sha256 074dfae859c3). Source of both verbatim quotations.
- Regulation (EU) No 648/2012, whole regulation, plain view dated 2012-07-04 — https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eur/2012/648/body/2012-07-04?view=plain (fetched 2026-11-23T12:29:49Z, sha256 7f7672cb7d7e). Corroborates the identical Art. 9(1)–(2) wording and supplies Art. 29(2) (CCP 10-year rule) used only to draw the distinction in §5.
- Article 9 as later amended (31 January 2020 and 31 December 2022 snapshots) — https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eur/2012/648/article/9/2020-01-31 (sha256 24f4dee031df) and https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eur/2012/648/article/9/2022-12-31 (sha256 3e6fbb06a4af). Used only to confirm in §5 that the two reported values are unchanged in later versions; they are **not** the basis of the answer.

*Out of scope by instruction and not relied on: Regulation (EU) No 2019/834 (EMIR Refit), Regulation (EU) 2024/2987 (EMIR 3), the level-2 regulatory/implementing technical standards on reporting, and any national implementing measures.*
